“The Hindus must have followed a system similar ot the equal ‘temperament’ system at present in vogue in Europe.”
“taṟkālam airōppāvil vaḻaṅki varum (Equal temperament) atāvatu curaṅkaḷukkiṭaiyil varum ciṟu curutikaḷaic cama iṭaiveḷikaḷuḷḷa pākaṅkaḷākap pirittal eṉṉum muṟaiyaiyē intukkaḷum vaḻaṅki vantirukka vēṇṭum.”
itil curaṅkaḷukku iṭaiyil varum curutikaḷaic cama iṭaiveḷi kaḷuṭaiyaṉa vāyp pirittal eṉṉum muṟaiyaiyē intukkaḷum vaḻaṅki vantirukka vēṇṭu meṉkiṟār. curaṅkaḷukku iṭaiyil varum ciṟu curutikaḷaic cama iṭaiveḷikaḷuṭaiyavaikaḷāyp pirikka vēṇṭu meṉṟirukkumāṉāl curaṅkaḷaiyum appaṭittāṉē pirittirukka vēṇṭum. curaṅkaḷaiyum curutiḷaiyum camamākap pirittu avaikaḷ oṉṟaṟ koṉṟu poruntum kaṇitamum colli yirukkiṟārkaḷeṉṟu itaṉ muṉ vistāramākap pārttōm. ippaṭic camamākap pirittu vaḻaṅkiya muṟai teṉṟamiḻ nāṭṭiṟku mikap pūrvamāṉatu. cumār 150, 120 varuṭaṅkaḷukku muṉ oru stāyiyil varum 12 curaṅkaḷaic camamākap pirittu avaṟṟai Equal temperament eṉṟu vaḻaṅkiṉārkaḷ. Equal temperament āṉa cama iṭaiveḷi kaḷuḷḷa paṉṉiraṇṭu curaṅkaḷōṭu cērntu vaḻaṅkum nuṭpac curaṅkaḷ iṉṉavai yeṉṟu aṟintu koḷḷāmaiyiṉāl palar palavitamākac colla nēriṭṭatu.
Mr. K.B.Deval,  nāratar kavaṉattiṟku vanta oḻuṅkāṉa iṭaiveḷikaḷuḷḷa ōcaiyaip pārkkilum ca; 1ri-84 2 ri-27, 3ri-71, 4ri-22, 1ka-90, 2ka-22 eṉṟu oḻuṅkīṉamāṉa ceṉṭskaḷai aḷavākak koṭukkiṟār. itu eṉṉa āccariyam. toṇṇūṟukkum irupattiraṇṭukkum eṉṉa oṟṟumai? eṇpattu nāṉkiṟkum irupattēḻiṟkum eṉṉa poruttam?
pūrvam intukkaḷ curutikaḷaic cama iṭaiveḷikaḷuṭaiyaṉavākap pirittārkaḷeṉṟu collukiṟavar tām koṭutta kaṇakkuc cama iṭaiveḷi kaḷuṭaiyaṉavalla veṉṟu ēṉ terintu koḷḷavillai? nāratar kavaṉattiṟku vanta oṉṟaiyum kavaṉittuc ceyta oṉṟaiyum ivar taḷḷalāmā? caṅkīta ratṉākarar riṣapattiṟkum kāntārattiṟkum mattima taivata niṣātaṅkaḷukkum nālu nālu curuti colla villaiyē. 2/3, 3/4 eṉṟa muṟaiyil avar curuti kaṇṭupiṭikkac collavillai. avar cila curutikaḷaik kūṭṭiyum kuṟaittuk koḷḷac collavumillai.
ippaṭip pala vitamāṉa oḻuṅkīṉaṅkaḷai oṉṟu cērttuc caṅkītat tiṟku utavi ceykiṟō meṉṟu nūl eḻutukiṟavarkaḷāl intiya caṅkītam keṭṭup pōkāmal eṉṉa ceyyum? ekkālattilum oru stāyiyil 22 curuti muṟaippaṭik kāṉamiruntatēyillai. caṅkīta ratṉākarar apip pirāyattaik karnāṭaka caṅkītattiṉ aṉupōkattōṭu iṇaikkap pārkkiṟa varkaḷiṉāl ivvāpattut tōṉṟiyirukkiṟatu. ippaṭippaṭṭavarkaḷāl pūrvamāṉa muṟaikaḷ varavara nuṭpam iḻantu māṟippōkiṉṟaṉa. aṭiyil varum vacaṉaṅkaḷāl avaikaḷaik kāṇpōm.
A.J.Hipkins.
“Under Captain Day’s guidance we find that in India an ancient quarter-tone system has become in modern times a half tone one, substantially our Equal temperament, but permitting an expressive or ornamental use of smaller intervals than the half-tone according to the players.”
“Captain Day colluvataik kavaṉittāl intiyāvil paḻamaiyāy vaḻaṅki vanta kāl curamuṟaiyāṉatu, taṟkālattil arai curamuṟaiyāy māṟiyirukkiṟatu. atai anēkamāy Equal temperament muṟaiyeṉṟē collalām. āṉāl anta araicura muṟaiyāṉatu vācippavarkaḷuṭaiya maṉōtarmattiṟkicaintapaṭi kamakamāyk kuṟaittum kūṭṭiyum nuṭpamāṉa curaṅkaḷāyc colluvataṟku iṭaṅ koṭukkiṟatu.”

pūrvam āyappālaiyil vaḻaṅki vanta curaṅkaḷ paṉṉiraṇṭē. appaṉṉiraṇṭum ca-pa vāy allatu iṇai, iṇaiyāy, ēḻāvatu, ēḻāvatu irāciyil paṉṉiru curaṅkaḷum poruntukiṉṟaṉa. itupōl aintāvatu aintāvatu irāciyil kiḷai kiḷaiyāy ca-ma vākap paṉṉiraṇṭu curaṅkaḷum kiṭaikkiṉṟaṉa. itai Equal temperament eṉṟu evvitattilum āṣcēpaṉai yiṉṟi nām collalāmē.
nātam cama iṭaiveḷikaḷuḷḷatāy illāmal Mr. Deval, colluvatupōla 84, 27, 71, 22, 90, 22 ceṉṭsukaḷāyiruntāl eppaṭip paṉṉiru curaṅkaḷum kiṭaikkum? pūrvatamiḻ makkaḷ vaḻaṅki vanta ivvuttama māṉa muṟai pallāyira varuṭaṅkaḷāka maṟaintu pōka paitākōras colliya 2/3, 3/4 eṉṟa muṭivu peṟāk kaṇakkum oru stāyiyil 22 curutikaḷeṉṟa iṭaṟukallum pala vittuvāṉkaḷuṭaiya maṉataik kalaṅka vaittaṉa.
pūrva tamiḻ makkaḷ āyappālaiyāṉa paṉṉiru araic curaṅkaḷilēyē kirakam māṟṟi irākaṅkaḷ pala uṇṭākkik kāṉam ceytu vantārkaḷ. vaṭṭappālaiyil 24 alaku allatu kāl cura muṟaiyākavum tirikōṇap pālaiyil araikkāl curamuṟaiyākavum caturappālaiyil vīcam curamuṟai yākavum pirittup paṉṉiru araic curaṅkaḷil oṉṟōṭu cērttuk kama kamāy vācittu vantārkaḷeṉṟu colliyirukkiṟōm. pūrva teṉṉintiya kāṉattil vaḻaṅki varum araiccura muṟaiyaiyum kālcura muṟaiyaiyum ivvaḷavāvatu kavaṉittārēyeṉṟu nām mikavum cantōṣappaṭak kūṭiyatāyirukkiṟatu.

teṉṉintiyāvil vaḻaṅki varum kāṉattil kāl curaṅkaḷaip pārkkilum araikkāl vīcam curaṅkaḷ atikamāy vaḻaṅki varukiṉṟaṉa veṉṟu kaṇṭiruppārāṉāl mikunta cantōṣamaṭain tiruppār. atōṭu ippōtu vaḻaṅkum nuṭpamāṉa curutikaḷaip paṟṟiyum colliyiruppār. oru stāyiyil 22 curutikaḷ varavēṇṭumeṉṟa kūkkuralukkuḷ ivar oru stāyiyil 24 curutikaḷ varukiṉṟaṉaveṉṟu coṉṉatu mikavum koṇṭāṭappaṭak kūṭiyatē.
itōṭu mēṟṟicai cāstirikaḷil piyāṉā curuti cērkkum muṟaiyai mikat teḷivāy eḻutiya Hermann Smith eṉpavaruṭaiya cila kuṟippukaḷaiyum iṅkē pārppatu mika nallateṉṟu tōṉṟukiṟatu. ivar curuti cērkkum muṟaiyaippaṟṟi oru puttakam eḻutiyirukkiṟār. atu taṟkālattil yāvarālum mika upayōkamāṉateṉṟu koṇṭāṭappaṭukiṟatu. nāḷatu varaiyum aṉuṣṭāṉattiliruntu varukiṟatu.
The art of tuning the Pianoforte by Hermann smith P.75, 76.
“Mr. W.H.B. Woolhouse remarks truly, “It is very misleading to suppose that the necessity of temperament applies only to instruments which have fixed tones. Singers and performers on perfect instruments must all temper their intervals, or they could not keep in tune with each other, or even with themselves; and on arriving at the same notes by different routes would be continually finding a want of agreement. The scale of Equal temperament obviates all such inconveniences, and continues to be universally accepted with unqualified satisfaction by the most eminent vocalists; and equally so by the most renowned and accomplished performers on stringed instruments, although these instruments are capable of an infinite variety of intonation. The high development of modern instrumental Music would not have been possible, and could not have been acquired, without the manifold advantages of the tempered intonation by equal semitones, and it has, in consequence, long become the established basis of tuning.”
Mr. Woolhouse  eṉpavar eṉṉa collukiṟār eṉṟāl, curaṅkaḷ stāpakamāyirukkappaṭṭa vāttiyaṅkaḷukkuttāṉ curaṅkaḷaic caripākamāyp pirikkummuṟai avaciyam, maṟṟavaikaḷukku avaciyamalla eṉṟu niṉaippatu picaku. pūraṇavāttiyaṅkaḷai vaittup pāṭupavarkaḷum, vācippavarkaḷum kūṭa taṅkaḷ curaṅkaḷ curutikkēṟka amaittuk koḷḷāviṭṭāl, maṟṟavarka ḷōṭu cērntu pāṭavāvatu tāṅkaḷē cutta curattil pāṭavāvatu kūṭātu. pala vaḻikaḷiṉ mūlamāy orē curaṅkaḷil vantu cēra vēṇṭiya avaciyam iruppatāl aṭikkaṭi vācippōrukkum pāṭuvōrukkum curavittiyācaṅkaḷ ēṟpaṭṭuk koṇṭēyirukkak kūṭiyatu. curutikaḷai camapākamākap pirittu stāpikkappaṭṭa ārōkaṇamāṉatu ivvita vittiyācaṅkaḷai uṇṭākka māṭṭātu. atuvē caṅkītam pāṭukiṟa vitvāṉkaḷ muṟai, vāttiyaṅkaḷ palavum palavitamāy curutiyēṟakkūṭiya vaiyāyirunta pōtilum tanti vāttiyaṅkaḷil nipuṇarāṉa ellā caṅkīta vitvāṉkaḷum cariyeṉṟu oppuk koḷḷum vaḻiyum ituvē. ippaṭi curaṅkaḷuk kiṭaiyiluḷḷa iṭai veḷikaḷai camapākaṅkaḷākap pirikkum muṟai ēṟpaṭṭa piṟakutāṉ caṅkīta vāttiyakāṉamāṉatu atikat tērcciyaṭaintirukkiṟatu mallāmal atuvē ellā vāttiyaṅkaḷaiyum curutikkēṟkak koṇṭuvarum muṟaiyeṉṟum atiṉāl uṇṭākum pirayōcaṉaṅkaḷ aṉantam eṉṟum yāvarālum oppuk koḷḷappaṭukiṟatu.
curaṅkaḷai cama ōcaiyuḷḷatākap pirikkum muṟai aṉu curaṅkaḷ cērttup pāṭuvataṟku utaviyāyiruppatu pōlavē taṉittup pāṭum oruvaṉukku mikunta pirayōcaṉamāyirukkiṟatu. pala vāttiyaṅkaḷ oṉṟu cērttup pāṭuvataṟkum tantivāttiyaṅkaḷil vācippataṟkum itu mikavum ēṟṟatāyirukkiṟatu. ituvē ellāt tērccikkum mūlakāraṇa māyirukkiṟateṉṟu collukiṟār. ivar collum Equal temperament muṟaiyāṉatu camīpa kālattil kaṇṭupiṭikkappaṭṭateṉṟu 69-m pakkattil colliyirukkiṟōm.
āṉāl immuṟaiyai ivarkaḷ kaṇṭupiṭippataṟku 100, 150 varuṭaṅkaḷukkumuṉ tañcāvūril iruntu koṇṭu pōṉa vīṇaiyil immuṟaippaṭic curuti cērttiruntatāka ūyayīva. ṉuyala collukiṟār eṉṟu muṉpu pārttirukkiṟōm. āṉāl laṇṭaṉ mīyūciyattil vaikkappaṭṭa tañcāvūr vīṇaikkup pala āyira varuṭaṅkaḷukku muṉṉā lēyē cama aḷavāṉa ōcaiyuṭaiyatāy nālu pālaikaḷil vaḻaṅkum nuṭpamāṉa curutikaḷaiyum kamakamāy vācikkakkūṭiyatāy pūrva tamiḻ makkaḷ kāṉam ceytu vantirukkiṟārkaḷ eṉṟu nām aṟikiṟōm. icaittamiḻil curuti cērkkum irakaciyam ivvaḷavu kālam maṟaintu ippoḻutāvatu namakkuk kiṭaittataṟkākac cantōṣappaṭa vēṇṭiyatāyirukkiṟatu.
tamiḻnāṭṭil oṉṟākiya cōḻa nāṭṭiliruntu koṇṭupōy laṇṭaṉ miyūciyattil vaikkappaṭṭa vīṇaiyiṉ cura aḷavukaḷ, mēl nāṭṭiṟku Equal temperament muṟaiyaik kāṇuvataṟku utaviyāyiruntirukku meṉṟu eṇṇukiṟēṉ.
The art of tuning the pianoforte by Hermann Smith, Page.17.
“The two cardinal points of the system are :
1. All octaves shall be tuned perfect.
2. All the fifths shall be a litle flatter than perfect.’
“piyāṉōviṉ nōṭṭukaḷai cariyāṉa curattil vaikkavēṇṭiyatil kavaṉikka vēṇṭiya iraṇṭu mukkiya kuṟippukaḷ.
(1) tuvakku nōṭṭum ataṟku eṭṭāvatu nōṭṭum cari porutta muḷḷavaiyāyirukka vēṇṭum.
(2) tuvakku nōṭṭum ataṟku aintāvatu nōṭṭum pūraṇa porutta millāmal caṟṟuk kuṟaittē vaikkappaṭa vēṇṭum.
nām ārampa curamāka vaittuk koḷḷum ātāra caṭcattiṟku mēluḷḷa eṭṭāvatu curamākiya caṭcam ātāra caṭcattōṭu evvitamum vittiyācamillāmal porunta vēṇṭum. oru ciṟu pālakaṉ patiṉāṟu vayatu paiyaṉōṭum patiṉāṟu vayatu paiyaṉ vayatāṉa oru maṉuṭaṉōṭum eppaṭi vaṭivattil porunti yiruppāṉō atēvitamāka ātāra caṭcamum mattiyastāyi caṭcamum tārastāyi caṭcamu mirukkiṉṟaṉa. manta cama ucca meṉṉum mūvakai iyakkilum oṉṟu, iraṇṭu, nālākap peruttirukkiṟatē yoḻiya vēṟalla. nāṟpaṭi araippaṭi yuḷḷum, araippaṭi oru paṭiyuḷḷum aṭaṅkukiṟatu eppaṭiyō appaṭiyē oṉṟaṟkoṉṟu miccamillāmal paṭippaṭiyāy uyarntu nātam oṉṟu paṭṭup porunti niṟkum.
ippaṭip porunti niṟkāmal pōṉāl oru stāyi cariyāy muṭintatāka eṇṇappaṭa māṭṭātu. oru vīṇait tantiyai iraṇṭu camapākamāka aḷantu pirittāl pirikkumiṭattil oru caṭcamikkiṟatu. muḻut tantiyiluḷḷa ōcaiyum iraṇṭākap piritta iṭattil varum ōcaiyum mikap porunti niṟkum. ivviraṇṭu curaṅkaḷum poruntāmaṟ pōṉāl eṭṭāvatu curam cariyāṉatalla.
ivveṭṭāvatu curattiṟkuḷḷāka varum iṭam oru stāyi eṉṟu collappaṭukiṟatu. iṉimēl ca-pa, ca-pa muṟaiyāy allatu aintāvatu aintāvatu curamāy (ca ri2 ka3 ma4 pa5) atāvatu pūrva tamiḻ muṟaippaṭi iṇai kiḷaiyāy allatu ēḻāvatu ēḻāvatu aintāvatu aintāvatu irāciyāyum kaṇṭupiṭittuk koṇṭupōkap paṉṉiru curaṅkaḷum varukiṉṟaṉa. paitākōras ca-pa 2/3 eṉṟu colvataiyum pārijātakkārar tantiyiṉ 1/3l pañcamam irukkiṟateṉṟu colvataiyum koṇṭu 2/3 x 2/3 ākak kaṇṭu piṭittuk koṇṭu pōvōmāṉāl atu paṉṉiraṇṭāvatu taṭavaiyil oru stāyikku mēṟpaṭṭup pōkiṟatai itaṉ muṉ kaṇakkil pārttirukkiṟōm. ākaiyiṉāl tantiyai mūṉṟil oṉṟākap pirittu anta aḷaviṉpaṭiyē 12 curaṅkaḷaik kaṇṭupiṭikka vēṇṭām. atu oru stāyiyil muṭivaṭaiyātu.
ākaiyiṉāl ovvoru taṭavaiyilum koñcam koñcam kuṟaittu oru stāyiyil pūraṇamāy muṭikiṟataṟ kēṟṟavitamāyc cērttuk koḷ eṉṟu collukiṟār. itaik koṇṭu 2/3 x 2/3 eṉṟa muṟaiyiṉāl kātukkup poruttamāṉa curam kiṭaikkāteṉṟu pirattiyaṭca māy aṟikiṟōm. itu pōlavē 3/4 x 3/4 āka varum ca-ma koñcam kuṟaintu varukiṟatiṉāl koñcam koñcam kūṭṭi oru stāyiyaic cariyāy muṭikka vēṇṭum eṉkiṟār. ca-pa muṟaiyil kuṟaittuc cērkkāmal pōṉāl kātiṟku aruvaruppāyirukkum eṉpataip paṟṟi aṭiyil varum vacaṉaṅkaḷil pārppōm.
The art of tuning the pianoforte by Hermann Smith, Page.54.
“These trials, as they are called, afford at each step a check by which the correctness of the progress may be indicated, or, untortunately, probably the incorrectness of your first estimates of “how much” and “how little.”
The last is the severest test, as the two notes of which this fifth is formed have been obtained by different series of fifths, and any imperfection in the gradation of the beatings allotted to the previous fifths will mainfest itself here. Hence this fifth, from the frequent harshness and howlings of its beats, has been technically termed the wolf, and strict injunctions are, “Look out for the wolf” Reekon yourself fortunate if no wolf appears.”
“inta nōṭṭukaḷait tirumpat tirumpa vācittup pārttāl evvaḷavu kūṭṭavēṇṭum ,evvaḷavu kuṟaikka vēṇṭum eṉpatu tiṭṭamākuvatu mallāmal nām nōṭṭukaḷaic cariyāṉa curattil vaikkiṟōmō allavō eṉṟum namakku niccayamākum. inta aintāvatu aintāvatāy (ca-pa poruttamāy) nōṭṭukaḷai curappaṭuttuvatu tāṉ atikak kaṣṭam. ēṉeṉṟāl mutalil itaik koñcam kūṭa vaittu viṭuvōmāṉāl atu varavara atikappaṭṭuk kaṭaiciyil peruṅkaṣṭattai viḷaivikkum. inta aintām poruttam kātukku iṉimaiyait tarāmal oru ōnāyiṉ ūḷaiyaippōl aṭikkaṭi iruppatāl ataṟku “ōnāy” eṉṟē peyar. piyāṉāvai ṟyūṉ paṇṇum oruvaṉukkuk koṭukkappaṭṭa mukkiya kaṭṭaḷai eṉṉaveṉṟāl “ōnāy varāmal jākkirataiyāyiru, appaṭi ōnāy varāviṭṭāl nī pākkiyavāṉtāṉ” eṉpatē.”

“But the scale used on the Vina since the 16th century, at least by one school viz., the Karnatic, has been temperament, except for any accidental defects in tuning. What circumstances led to the adoption of this scale will have to be discussd on a future occasion. But it may be remarked here that this temperate scale is a capital discovery and the Hindus deserve to be congratulated on it, unless indeed it was borrowed like many other things in music from the Persians and Arabs. If any Indian perceives the Vina music to be defective, now that he has been made aware that its scale is one of equal temperament, let him taboo the instrument altogether or introduce modifications which will allow of the use of what he thinks to be a better scale.”

Ancient Indians in Mesopotamia.
History repeats itself in the strangest manner. This is not the first time that Indians (now forming the Expeditionary Force) are playing an important part in altering the history of the fertile valley drained by the waters of the Tigris and Euphrates. Archaeological researches have tended towards the establishment of the most remarkable fact that colonists from ancient India in remote ages settled in Mesopotamia.
What leading part they played in that cradle of civilisation will be realised when itis stated that an eminent archaeologist of great experience, after patient studies, is inclined to come to the starting conclusion that the wonderful Mesopotamian culture displayed by the ancient Babylonians and Assyrians was derived from the Sumerians. These were no other than Dravidian settlers from India, who had migrated to the head of the Persian Gulf at the very dawn of civilisation.
Mr. H.R. Hall, of the British Museum, thus expresses the latest views on the origin of the Sumerians, who were the pioneers of the high degree of civilisation to which the ancient nations of the Euphrates valley attained :-
The Sumerian culture springs into our view ready-made, as it were, which is what we should expect if it was, as seems on other grounds probable, brought into Mesopotamia from abroad. The earliest scenes of their culture development had, perhaps, not been played upon the Babylonian stage at all, but in a different country away across the Persian mountains to the eastward.
The ethnic type of the Sumerians, so strongly marked in their statues and reliefs, was a s different from those of the races which surrounded them as was their language from those of the Semites. Aryans or others, they were decidedly Indian in type. The face-type of the average Indian of to-day is, no doubt, much the same as that of his race ancestors thousands of years ago. And it is by no means improbable that the Sumerians were an Indian race which passed, certainlyby land, perhaps, also by sea through Persia to the valley of the Two Rivers. It was in the Indian home (perhaps the Indus Valley) that we suppose for them that their culture developed.
There their writing may have been invented, and progressed from purely pictorial to a simplified and abbreviated form which afterwards in Babylonia took on its peculiar “cuneiform” appearance owing to its being written with a square ended stylus on soft clay. There is little doubt that India must have been one of the earliest centres of human civilisation, and it seems natural to suppose that the strange un-Semitic un-Aryan people, who came from the East to civilise the West, were of Indian origin, especially when we see with our eyes how very Indian the Sumerians were in type.
The origin of the Dravidian race, the most primitive of the Indian types, is lost in obscurity. No satisfactory theory has yet been forthcoming to point out their original home (if they had any other than India) from which they migrated. Huxley’s theory as to their connection with the aborigines of Australia, although apparently supported by Sclater’s hypothesis of a vast continent now submerged under the Indian Ocean, which once embraced Africa, India and Australia, has been traversed by Sir William Turner’s comparative studies of the Australian and Dravidian crania.
Sir W.W. Hunter’s assumption,  which assigned a trans-Himalayan origin to the Dravidians, has been discounted for various reasons. The failure of all theorists to assign a foreign home to the Dravidians appears to justify the conclusion that they were among the original inhabitants of India.
There is every reason to suppose that pre-Aryan Dravidian culture flourished in their great home, well-endowed as it was by bountiful Nature. Whether the Dravidians from India who migrated to Mesopotamia were compelled to seek a new home forced by famine or by persecution, or whether they were traders or adventurers, we have no means of ascertaining. We are also in the dark as to whether they took the difficult land route across Baluchistan and Persia or they went by sea along the coast.
The presence of the Brahuis in Baluchistan, who have a dialect showing strong affinity with the Dravidian languages, appears to lend much support to the former theory, specially when we take into consideration the fact that their ancestral neighbours who inhabited ancient Persia, most probably belonged to the Dravidian race.
These ancient non-Aryan inhabitants of Persia were called “Anarikoi” by the Greeks which is undoubtedly a corrupted form of “Anarya.” by which name the Dravidians were known to the first Aryan settlers in India.
Several years ago, Mr. Hewitt pointed out that the Euphrates valley was the home of the Hindu lunar astronomy, which was introduced into India before 4700 B.C. He also produced evidence pointing to the existence of trade relations between India and Mesopotamia in very ancient times.
The discovery of indigo and muslin in Egyptian tombs conclusively showed that Indian products found their way into Egypt so long ago as at least 1700 B.C. There is also evidence that the Sumerians traded in teak and muslin, which were exclusive products of India. Mr. Hewitt was of opinion that these commercial transactions between Western India and Sumer took place in 6000 B.C. He also endeavoured to trace the presence of Sumerians in ancient Gujarat, Later researches have not only confirmed some of the conclusions of Mr. Hewitt, but, as we find from the above quotation from a leading authority on archaeology and ancient history, the identification of the Sumerians with the ancient Dravidians of India leaves little room for doubt.
The linguistic evidence as supplied by the Brahuis of the survival of a Dravidian language in the remote central highlands of Baluchistan forms a strong link for establishing the identity of the Sumerians. If the opinion of Dr. Grierson to the effect that of all Dravidians the Brahuis alone retain the true ethnic type owing to their isolation, be accepted, then we are led to the conclusion that the Sumerians were imigrants from Southern India as is evidenced from their strong resemblance to the Dravidian ethnic type as modified by admixture with aboriginal nationalities.
If the Brahuis really represent the true Dravidian ethnic type, an althernative theory may be proposed pointing to Baluchistan as the original home from which a great Dravidian emigration to India took place in very ancient times.
The recent geological investigations of Mr. Vredenburg appears to favour such a hypothesis, as there is now good reason to surmise, on the basis of Mr. Vredenburg’s explorations, that the desert tracts of Baluchistan were once covered by fertile lands which were well populated. The exhaustion of the water resources and consequent production of famine conditions threatened the ancient inhabitants, rendering migration on a vast scale imperative.
That the Sumerians who settled in Southern Babylonia (Sumer) were the founders of Babylonian culture is abundantly shown by the relics recovered by archaeologists from the excavation conducted on the sites of the ancient cities. The early history of Babylonia is a record of Sumerian domination and progress.
The excavations of the city mounds at the lowest levels disclose Sumerian culture so advanced that the people were already using copper. The Sumerian copper implements found at Tello in Babylonia, probably go so far back as 4000, B.C. A bronze statuette of Gudea, perhaps the greatest of all the Sumerian Kings, dating back to 2500 B.C., is a landmark in the history of the antiquity of copper.
More than one eminent archaeologist has advanced the opinion that India was the first home of the bronze industry. Even such a conservative historian as Mr. Vincent Smith admits that copper was used in India in very ancient times. Some of the prehistoric copper implements (probably dating back to about 2000. B.C.) of the most remarkable board discovered in 1870 at Gungeria, in the Central Provinces, bear a close resemblance to those found in Babylonia.
Although very valuable work has been done in Southern India by Mr. Rhea by his discoveries of prehistoric metal implements, a great deal has yet to be done in this direction in the way of discovery and serious study to throw light on the ancient history of metallurgy in India and its possible connection with Mesopotamian Culture.
The Sumerians were great builders of towns and irrigation works. They were the first town-planners known to history. They developed the City State to a marked extent. Each city had its temple with a city god, who was the owner of all the city land. Every city was governed by a hereditary ruler, who was also the high priest of the local god with the title of “patesi” or vicegerent of the god. We do not known much about the Sumerian deities.
Nippur, which was the chief city of ancient Babylonia, had a great temple dedicated to Ennil. The identity of this name with the Dravidian name for the Moon god is significant. The corresponding Dravidian name, Bal is most prominent in Babylonian mythology.
The temple at Nippur was a great repository for votive offerings of the Sumerian Kings which have yielded valuable material for ancient history, showing that the Sumerians who lived 6,000 years before us lived in great an populous cities under organised civil and religious government.
They had long ago emerged from the savage state, as they were already using metal and had their own system of writing. From their statues we see them with shaven heads and wearing long garments. Their physiognomy and fashions of dress bear such close resemblance to the Dravidian that their common origin is not improbable, as such striking similarity cannot be merely accidental.
Dr. Buhler traced the derivation of the ancient Brahui script, the parent of most of the known alphabets of India from Mesopotamia, fixing the date of its introduction into India at about 800 B.C.
It is acknowledged by some authorities that the Tamil alphabet, with its peculiar characters of a primitive type, was  in existence long before the introduction of Brahui or Kharosthi. The supposition that the Tamil alphabet was derived from a Semitic source and is a variety of the Aramaic or Hymiaritic script which originated in Mesopotamia ought to undergo modification in the light of recent researches which appear to reverse the country of origin of the Tamil alphabet.
When another Champollion is found to unearth the deeply buried relics of the ancient Dravidian culture, in all probability it will be discovered that lunar astronomy as well as the very first alphabet originated in India just as it is now being recognised that the advanced civilisation of ancient Mesopotamia owed its inception to the Sumerians from India. How far the world is thus indebted to the ancient Dravidians, as appears to be disclosed by recent researches is a subject which finds no place in the works of the modern historians of ancient India.

āti pāpilōṉiyāviṉ mukkiya nakarākiya nippūril Ennil eṉṟa teyvattukkup piratiṣṭai ceyyappaṭṭa oru ālayam iruntatu. inta eṉṉil eṉṉum pērāṉatu tirāviṭa pāṣaiyil cantiraṉukkup pērākiya nilā eṉṉum vārttaiyai ottiruppatu kavaṉikkappaṭattakkatu. itaṟkuc camamāṉa tirāviṭap pērākiya pāl eṉpatu pāpilōṉiya pūrva carittirattil upayōkikkap paṭṭirukkiṟatu.
nippūr nakariluḷḷa inta ālayattil cumēriya rājākkaḷ taṅkaḷ teyvattukkuc celuttum kāṇikkaikaḷellām oṉṟu cērttu vaikkappaṭṭiruntaṉa. avaikaḷai ārāyumiṭattu pūrva carittirattukku utaviyāṉa anēka kāriyaṅkaḷai aṅkē kāṇalām. avaikaḷiliruntu nām aṟikiṟateṉṉa veṉṟāl namakku 6000 varuṣaṅkaḷukku muṉṉuḷḷa antac cumēriyarkaḷ periyatum jaṉanerukka muḷḷatumāṉa nakaraṅkaḷil vacittārka ḷeṉṟum annakaraṅkaḷil civil viṣayattukkum mataviṣayattukkumāṉa rājyattukkuriya amcaṅkaḷ anēkam iruntaṉa veṉṟum terikiṟatu.
avarkaḷ ulōkaṅkaḷai upayōkittataiyum taṅkaḷukkeṉṟu uṇṭākkiṉa pāṣaiyiṉ eḻuttukkaḷaiyum kavaṉikkumpōtu avarkaḷ veku kālattukku muṉ nākarīkattai yaṭaintiruntār kaḷeṉṟum terikiṟatu. avarkaḷ cilaikaḷaip pārttāl avarkaḷ talai mayirai cirait tiruntatākavum nīṇṭa aṅki pōṉṟa vastiraṅkaḷai upayōkittatākavum terikiṟatu. avarkaḷ mukarūpamum, uṭaiyum - tirāviṭaruṭaiya rūpattaiyum uṭaiyaiyum ottiruppatāl avarkaḷ orē jātiyar eṉṟu cantēkamaṟac collalām. avvaḷavu tūram anēka viṣayaṅkaḷil iruvarum ottiruppatāṉatu taṟceyalāy uṇṭāṉatu eṉṟu colla muṭiyātu. intiyāviluḷḷa anēkam pāṣai eḻuttukkaḷukkut tāyākiya Brahui eḻuttāṉatu mecōp pottāmiyāviliruntu uṟpattiyāṉatāyum atu intiyāviṟku ki.mu.800-m varuṣattil koṇṭu varappaṭṭateṉṟum Dr. Buhler eṉpavar collukiṟār.
āṉāl maṟṟavarkaḷ collukiṟateṉṉaveṉṟāl tamiḻp pāṣai yiṉ eḻuttukaḷ atiṉ atipūrvamāṉa eḻuttukaḷiṉ rūpattaik kavaṉikkum pōtu Brahui allatu Karosthi pāṣaiyiṉ eḻuttukaḷukku muṉṉālēyē intiyāvil iruntatāka niṉaikkiṟārkaḷ. tamiḻp pāṣaiyiṉ eḻuttukkaḷ cemiṟṟik pāṣaiyiliruntu uṟpattiyāṉa aramēyik allatu ham yāriṭṭik pāṣaiyiliruntu mecōppottāmiyāvil uṇṭāyiṉa eṉṟu collum apippirāyattait taṟkāla carittira ārāycci nēril colva tōṭu ottup pārkkumpōtu atu cariyāṉatākat tōṟṟavillai. uṇmai itaṟku etirmāṟāka irukka vēṇṭum.
Champollion  eṉpavarai pōlotta iṉṉoru nipuṇar ulakattil tōṉṟi āti tirāviṭaruṭaiya nākarīkamum nilaimaiyum iṉṉateṉṟu pūrṇamāy veḷippaṭum kālattil pūrva mecōppottāmiyāruṭaiya virttiyāṉa nākarīkam intiyāviliruntu aṅku vantu kuṭiyēṟiṉa cumēriyarāl uṇṭāṉatu eṉṟu yāvarum oppuk koḷvatu pōlavē vāṉa cāstiramum ātipāṣaiyiṉ eḻuttukaḷ mutaliya nākarīka ciṉṉaṅkaḷum intiyāvil mutal mutal ārampamāṉateṉṟu oppuk koḷḷappaṭum.
āṉāl taṟkāla carittira ārāycciyaik kavaṉikkumpōtu āti ulaka māṉatu tirāviṭa jātiyārukku ivvaḷavu tūram kaṭamaippaṭṭiruntatu eṉṟa caṅkatiyai pūrva intiyāvaip paṟṟip pēcum taṟkāla carittirakkārar eṭuttuc collakkūṭa māṭṭārkaḷ eṉṟu terikiṟatu.
A. kōs.
mēṟkāṭṭiya cila vacaṉaṅkaḷiṉāl mecōp pottāmiyāvil kuṭiyēṟiṉa pūrva intiyarkaḷiṉ cila mukkiya kuṟippukkaḷai iṅkē kāṇkiṟōm. mecōp pottāmiyā eṉpatu ciṉṉāciyāvil tikirīs aipirāttu natikaḷ ōṭum ceḻippāṉa piratēcattiṟkup peyarāy vaḻaṅki vantirukkiṟatu. aipirāttu nati ātiyil ulaka ciruṣṭip piṉ kālattil ētēṉ eṉṟa tōṭṭattil pāyntu koṇṭirunta nati eṉṟu collap paṭukiṟatu. innatikaḷ pāyum iṭamāṉatu mikunta ceḻippuṭaiyatāy anēka paḻa varkkaṅkaḷum kāy, kaṟi, tāṉiyaṅkaḷum viḷaiyak kūṭiya nāṭāyirunta teṉṟu carittiraṅkaḷ mūlamāyp pārttirukkiṟōm.
intukkaḷukkuc cumēriyar eṉṟu peyar. ivarkaḷ muka uruvattilum tēkak kaṭṭuppāṭṭilum intiyāviṉ teṉpākattilirunta tirāviṭa jāti yārai ottiruntārkaḷ. ivarkaḷ intiyāviṉ teṉpākattiliruntu aṅkē pōyk kuṭiyēṟiyirukka vēṇṭum. ivarkaḷ paḻakka vaḻakkaṅkaḷilum tērcci peṟṟirunta kalaikaḷilum intiyāviṉ teṉpākattilirunta varkaḷai ottiruppataik koṇṭu teṉṉintiyāviliruntē vantirukka vēṇṭum. pāpilōṉ, acīriyā eṉṉum pūrva kālattu rājyaṅkaḷai stāpittavarkaḷākavum avaṟṟai āṇṭavarkaḷākavum, ciṟpacāstiram, vāṉacāstiram mutaliya kalaikaḷilum, tuṇi neytal cāyamēṟṟutal, payiriṭutal, ulōkaṅkaḷāl cilai vārttal mutaliya kaittoḻilkaḷilum varttakattilum mikat tērntavarkaḷākavum iruntārkaḷ.
ki.mu.6000 varuṭaṅkaḷukku muṉṉālēyē cumēriyarukkum teṉṉinti yarukkum varttaka campantamiruntatākac collappaṭukiṟatu.ki.mu.4700 varuṭaṅkaḷukku muṉ mecōppottāmiyā nāṭṭiṟku intiyāviliruntē vāṉacāstiram koṇṭupōkappaṭṭatākak kāṇkiṟōm. pelujiḵtāṉ malai nāṭṭilum pāracīkattilum pēcappaṭum pāṣai tirāviṭa pāṣaiyā yiruntatiṉāl akkuṭikaḷ pūrvam intiyāviliruntu pōyirukka vēṇṭu meṉṟu eṇṇa iṭamirukkiṟatu. avarkaḷ pēci vanta pāṣai pirakūys pāṣaiyeṉṟu aḻaikkappaṭṭatu. ciṉṉāciyāvukkuc camīpamāṉa it tēcaṅkaḷil tirāviṭarkaḷ kuṭiyēṟiṉārkaḷeṉṟum avarkaḷ tirāviṭa pāṣai pēciṉārkaḷeṉṟum collappaṭukiṟatu. ivarkaḷaik kirēkkar ‘anāriyā’ eṉṟu aḻaittārkaḷ.
cumēriyarāl ceyyappaṭṭa pittaḷai āyutaṅkaḷum veṇkala cāmāṉkaḷum pāpilōṉ nāṭṭiluḷḷa tellō eṉṉum nakaril veṭṭi yeṭukkappaṭṭaṉa. ivai ki.mu. 4000 varuṭaṅkaḷukku muṉṉuḷḷavai yeṉat terikiṟatu.
cumēriya aracarkaḷil ciṟantavaṉākiya kuṭiyā eṉpavaṉuṭaiya veṇkalac cilaiyāṉatu ki.mu.2000 varuṭaṅkaḷukku muṉṉuḷḷa cilaiyākak kāṇappaṭukiṟatu. itaṉāl intiyarkaḷ mikap pūrvattil pittaḷai vēlai ceyvatilum vārppiṭaṅkaḷ ceyvatilum tērntavarkaḷāyiruntārkaḷeṉṟu tōṉṟukiṟatu. itōṭu 1870-m varuṣam mattiya mākāṇattiluḷḷa kaṅkariyā eṉṉum iṭattil veṭṭiyeṭukkappaṭṭa pittaḷai āyutaṅkaḷ pūrvam pāpi lōṉil veṭṭiyeṭukkappaṭṭa āyutaṅkaḷai ottirukkiṉṟaṉa. ivaikaḷ ki.mu.2000 varuṭaṅkaḷukku muṉ upayōkikkap paṭṭavaiyeṉṟu terikiṟatu.
cumēriyar kaṭṭaṭam kaṭṭuvatilum nilaṅkaḷukku nīrppāyccuvatilum mikat tērntavarkaḷ. ciṟpa cāstirattiṉpaṭi paṭṭaṇaṅkaḷ kōṭṭaikaḷ ālayaṅkaḷ kaṭṭuvatilum ālayap paṇiviṭaikaḷ ceyvatilum tērntirun tārkaḷeṉṟum avaṟṟil ivarkaḷaiyē mutalvarākac collalām eṉṟum kāṇappaṭukiṟatu.
pāpilōṉ rājyattiṉ mukkiya nakarākiya nippūril eṉṉil eṉṉum teyvamāṉatu iruntatākavum atu tirāviṭa pāṣaiyil cantiraṉukkup peyarākiya nilā eṉṟa vārttaikkuc cariyāyirukkiṟatākavum av vārttaikkuc camamāṉa pāl eṉṉum tirāviṭap peyar pāpilōṉiṉ pūrva carittirattil upayōkikkap paṭṭiruppatākavum terikiṟatu. atōṭu avarkaḷ teyva paktiyil ciṟantavarkaḷākavum naṭai uṭai pāvaṉaikaḷil nākarīka muṭaiyavarkaḷākavu miruntārkaḷeṉṟu kāṇkiṟōm.
avarkaḷ pēci vanta pāṣaiyāṉatu pirakūys eṉṟu aḻaikkappaṭṭa teṉṟum avveḻuttukkaḷ pāpilōṉiṉ kaṭṭaṭaṅkaḷiluḷḷa ceṅkal kaḷil kāṇappaṭukiṉṟaṉa veṉṟum collukiṟār. avveḻuttukkaḷ tamiḻ pāṣaiyiṉ eḻuttukkaḷākavē yirukkiṉṟaṉaveṉṟum avai cemiṭṭik pāṣaiyiliruntu uṟpattiyāṉa aramēyik pāṣaiyiliruntu uṇṭāka villaiyeṉṟum collappaṭukiṟatu.
mēṟkaṇṭa kuṟippukaḷ anēka pūrva carittira ārāyccikkārariṉ apip pirāyaṅkaḷaip paricōtittu eḻutappaṭṭatāka nām kāṇpōm. ivvapip pirāyaṅkaḷai aṉucaritta cila kuṟippukaḷai itaṉ muṉ mutalām pākattil kaṇṭirukkiṟōm. ikkuṟippukkaḷiṉāl piraḷayattiṟku muṉṉālēyē teṉ maturaiyil aracāṭciyirunta kālattil pāṇṭiyarāja vamcattaic cērnta varkaḷum maṟṟum kuṭikaḷumākiya pūrva tamiḻ makkaḷ mecōppottāmi yāvukkup pōyirukka vēṇṭumeṉṟum atiliruntu pāpilōṉ, acīriyā mutaliya rājyaṅkaḷai stāpittu aṅkē aracāṭci ceytirukka vēṇṭu meṉṟum niṉaikka ētuvirukkiṟatu.
cantira vamcattaic cērntavarkaḷāyiruntatiṉāl tāṅkaḷ aṅkē kaṭṭiṉa pāpilōṉ eṉṉum paṭṭaṇattilirunta eṉṉil eṉṉum teyvat tiṟkum ippeyar koṭuttiruppārkaḷeṉṟu niṉaikka iṭamirukkiṟatu.
piḻaippataṟku valacai vāṅkiya kuṭikaḷ periya paṭṭaṇaṅkaḷaiyum kōṭṭaikaḷaiyum kaṭṭi mikap pirapalamāyirunta rājyaṅkaḷai stāpippatu kūṭiya kāriyamalla. avarkaḷ teṉ pāṇṭi nāṭṭil aracāṭci ceytu koṇṭu vanta rājarkaḷāyāvatu rāja vamcattārkaḷāyāvatu irukka vēṇṭum. pāpilōṉ eṉṉum paṭṭaṇam aipirāttu āṟṟiṉ irukarai yilum 225 caturamail parappuṭaiyatāyc cuṟṟilum 75 aṭi uyaramum 32 aṭi akalamumāṉa kōṭṭaiyum peṉṉam periya 120 veṇkalak katavukaḷu muṭaiyatāyk kaṭṭappaṭṭiruntateṉṟum ataṉ naṭumattiyil rāja araṇ maṉaiyum kōvilum kaṭṭappaṭṭiruntaṉaveṉṟum maṟṟum āccariyappaṭat takkavaikaḷum amaikkap paṭṭiruntaṉaveṉṟum ipputtakattiṉ ārampattil colliyirukkiṟōm.
avaikaḷil kaṇṭa kuṟippukaḷai nām pārkkumpoḻutu vāṉmīka muṉivar “navamaṇikaḷ iḻaittatāyp poṉṉāṟ ceyyappaṭṭatāyk kōṭṭai matil cuvarkaḷōṭu iṇaikkappaṭṭatāṉa pāṇṭiyaṉ kōṭṭai vācaṟkatavukaḷaik kāṇpīrka” ḷeṉṟu vāṉara cēṉaikaḷukkuc coṉṉa teṉ maturaiyiṉ alaṅkārattiṟ kottavaikaḷāy avaikaḷ kāṇappaṭu kiṉṟaṉa.
teṉ maturaiyiṉ nākarīkamum ataṉ aḻakum colliyirukkum ākāsvēru rājaṉ viruntiṉ perumaikkēṟṟa vitamākavē iruntirukka vēṇṭum. intiyā mutal ettiyōppiyā varaiyumuḷḷa 127 nāṭukaḷai aracāṇṭu vantāṉ eṉṟu colvatai nām kavaṉikkumpoḻutu ivaṉirunta cūcāṉ paṭṭaṇamum antap paṭṭaṇattaic cērnta pāracīka tēcamum oru kālattil teṉmaturaiyilirunta pāṇṭiyarāja vamcattōr veḷināṭukaḷukkuc ceṉṟu kaṭṭi āṇṭirunta irājyaṅkaḷāka iruttal vēṇṭumeṉat tōṉṟukiṟatu.
intiyāviṉ vaṭa ellaiyāyirukkum imayamalai varaiyum teṉ pāṇṭi nāṭṭaracarkaḷ āṇṭukoṇṭu vantirukkiṟārkaḷeṉṟum avarkaḷuk kuriya mīṉakkoṭi imayamalaiyil āṭik koṇṭiruntateṉṟum cācaṉaṅkaḷil kāṇkiṟōm.
pāpilōṉ rājyattiṟkum ataic cērnta pala rājyaṅkaḷukkum talainakaraṅkaḷākiya ērēk, akkāt, kalṉē eṉṉum iṭaṅkaḷaiyum acīriya rājyattaic cērntavaikaḷākiya niṉivē, rekōpōt, kālāku, rēcēṉ eṉṉum paṭṭaṇaṅkaḷaiyum kaṭṭiya nimirōttaip paṟṟi nām itaṉmuṉ pārttirukkiṟōm. ivaikaḷ ciṉṉāciyāviṉ teṉpuṟamāy tikirīs aipirāttu eṉṉum natikaḷ pāyum mocōp pottāmiyā nāṭākavum ataṟkuc camīpattiluḷḷa iṭaṅkaḷākavu mirukkiṉṟaṉa.
mocōppottāmiyā nāṭṭil cumēriyar aracāṭci ceytu koṇṭiruntārkaḷeṉṟum ivarkaḷ teṉṉintiyāviliruntavarkaḷeṉṟum ivarkaḷ pelujistāṉ vaḻiyāy vantu pelujistāṉattilum pāracīkattilum taṅkiṉārkaḷeṉṟum ivarkaḷ pēciya pāṣai pirakūys pāṣai eṉṟu collappaṭum tamiḻāyiruntateṉṟum avveḻuttukkaḷ pūrva tamiḻ eḻuttāyiruntaṉaveṉṟum colvatai nām kavaṉikkaiyil pūrvam teṉpāṇṭi nāṭṭiluḷḷa tamiḻ makkaḷ oru kālattil imayamalai varaiyilum ataṟ kappāl peljistāṉ pāracīkam, mecōppottāmiyā mutaliya iṭaṅkaḷilum palapala rājyaṅkaḷai stāpittu āṇṭu vantārka ḷeṉṟum intiyā mutal ettiyōppiyā varaiyumuḷḷa 127 nāṭukaḷil rājyapāram ceytārkaḷeṉṟum kāṇkiṟōm.
itaṉāl inta 127 nāṭukaḷilum mutal mutal tamiḻpāṣaiyē pēcap paṭṭu vantateṉṟum ataṉpiṉ pāṣaikaḷ citaivuṟṟu vevvēṟu peyar kaḷuṭaṉ aḻaikkappaṭṭirukka vēṇṭumeṉṟum avaikaḷil miccamāṉa vārttaikaḷ tamiḻ vārttaikaḷāyiruppatiṉāl ivvuṇmaiyaik kāṇalāmeṉṟum terikiṟatu.
tamiḻp pāṣai pēci vanta ivarkaḷiṭamiruntē akkampakkattiliruntē maṟṟavar ciṟpa cāstiram, cōtiṭa cāstiram, caṅkīta cāstiram, vaittiya cāstiram mutaliya kalaikaḷaip paṭittirukka vēṇṭum eṉṟu tōṉṟukiṟatu. vāṉa cāstirattiṉ nuṭpattaiyum, caṅkīta cāstirattiṉ nuṭpattaiyum nām kavaṉippōmāṉāl avaikaḷ mikap pūrvamāyt teṉ maturaiyil vaḻaṅkit tērcci peṟṟiruntaṉaveṉṟum pēṇuvāraṟṟamaiyāl nāḷaṭaivil kuṟaintaṉaveṉṟum terikiṟatu.
itōṭu cattiya vētam ātiyākamam 10-m atikāram 2 mutal 5 vākkiyaṅkaḷaik kavaṉikkaiyil yāppēttiṉ kumārarkaḷ ēḻu peyar. yāppāttiṉ kumārar kōmar, yāvāṉiṉ kumārarkaḷ ēḻu peyarkaḷum avarkaḷ peyarāl uṇṭāṉa vevvēṟu jātikaḷum avarkaḷ tīvukaḷum pāṣaikaḷum avarkaḷuṭaiya tēcaṅkaḷum evvēḻāyiruppatākak kāṇap paṭukiṟatu. avai varumāṟu :
“yāppēttiṉ kumārar, kōmar, mākōku, mātāy, yāvāṉ, tūpāl, mēcēkku, tīrās eṉpavarkaḷ.
kōmāriṉ kumārar, askiṉās, rīppāttu, tokarmā eṉpavarkaḷ.
yāvāṉiṉ kumārar elīcā, tarṣīs, kittīm, totāṉīm eṉpavarkaḷ.
ivarkaḷāl jātikaḷuṭaiya  tīvukaḷ  avaṉavaṉ pāṣaiyiṉ paṭiyēyum avaravarkaḷ kōttirattiṉ paṭiyēyum jātiyiṉ paṭiyēyum vēṟu vēṟu tēcaṅkaḷāy pakukkappaṭṭaṉa.”
yāppēttiṉ ēḻu kumārarkaḷum ēḻu jātikaḷāṉārkaḷeṉṟum avarkaḷ ēḻu tīvukaḷiliruntārkaḷeṉṟum avarkaḷ ovvoruvarumirunta ovvoru tīvum evvēḻu tēcaṅkaḷāka vakukkappaṭṭateṉṟum niṉaikka iṭamirukkiṟatu. itaṉāl lemūriyā eṉṟu aḻaikkappaṭṭa teṉ maturai nāṭu ēḻu tīpaṅkaḷākavum ovvoru tīpamum evvēḻu nāṭākavumiruntatai annāṭṭiliruntu jalappiraḷayattiṟkut tappip pōṉavarkaḷ oruvāṟu taṅkaḷ ñāpakattiṟkāka ippaṭip pirittirippārkaḷeṉṟu collavum iṭamirukkiṟatu. itaṉāl pūrva tamiḻ vaḻakkam pēṇappaṭṭu vantatāka nām eṇṇa vēṇṭum.
tamiḻ makkaḷ piraḷayattiṟkut tappi ōṭiya kālattil pala iṭaṅkaḷukkup pōyk kuṭi yēṟiṉārkaḷeṉṟum rājāṅka muṟaiyāyp pala iṭaṅkaḷai jeyittu rājyaṅkaḷ stāpittārkaḷeṉṟum collalām.
itaṉāl intiyā mutal ettiyōppiyā tēcam varaiyiluḷḷa 127 nāṭukaḷ tamiḻarkaḷ aracāṭciyilirunta teṉṟum tamiḻp pāṣai pēcappaṭṭu vanta teṉṟum terikiṟatu. inta 127 nāṭukaḷum intiyāviṉ teṉ kōṭi mutal āppirikkāviṉ teṉ kōṭi varaiyumuḷḷa ārēpiyāk kaṭaliṉ cuṟṟōramāyirukkak kāṇpōm.

The Popular Encyclopedia Vol I Page 370.
“The advanced condition of the Assyrians in various in  other respects is sufficiently evidenced by the representations on the sculptures, and by the remains discovered among their ruined buildings. We now know that they understood and applied the arch; that they constructed tunnels, aqueducts and drains; that they used the lever and the roller; that they engraved gems in a hightly artistic way; that they understood the arts of inlaying, enamelling and overlaying with metals; that they manufactured porcelain and transparent and coloured glass and were acquainted with the lens; that they possessed vases, jars, and other dishes, bronze and ivory ornaments, bells, gold earrings and bracelets of excellent design and workmanship.
Their household furniture also gives us a high idea of their skill, taste, minuteness, and accuracy.
The cities of Nineveh, Assur and Arbela had each their royal observatories superintended by astronomers royal, who had to send in their reports to the king twice a month.
At an early date the stars were numbered and named, a calendar was formed in which the year was divided into twelve months (of thirty days each) called after the Zodical signs, but as this division was found to be inaccurate an intercalary month was added every six years. The week was divided into seven days, the seventh being a day of rest; the day was divided into twelve casbu of two hours each, each casbu being subdivided into sixty minutes, and these again into sixty seconds.
Eclipses were recorded from a very remote epoch, and their recurrence roughly determined. The principal astronomical work, called the Illumination of Bel, was compiled for the library of Sargon of Agane; it was inscribed on seventy tablets, and went through numerous editions one of the latest being in the British Museum.
It treats among other things on observations of Comets, the polar star, the conjunction of the Sun and Moon and the motions of Venus and Mars. The study of mathematics was fairly advanced, and the people who were acquainted with the sun-dial, the clepsydra, the pully, and the lever must have had considerable knowledge of Mechanics.”
“maṟṟum anēka kāriyaṅkaḷilum acīriyar atika tērcciyaṭaintirun tārkaḷ eṉpatu kaṟkaḷil kāṇappaṭum cilaikaḷiṉālum avarkaḷuṭaiya pāḻāyppōṉa nakaraṅkaḷil kāṇappaṭum kaṭṭaṭaṅkaḷiṉālum rucuvākiṟatu. avarkaḷaip paṟṟi nām ippōtu aṟivateṉṉa veṉṟāl ārc eṉṉap paṭṭa vaḷaivai avarkaḷ aṟintum upayōkittu miruntārkaḷ; ṭaṉṉalkaḷai veṭṭiṉārkaḷ; nīrōṭum vāykkālkaḷaiyum cākkaṭaikaḷai yum kaṭṭiṉārkaḷ; līvar rōlar ivaikaḷiṉ upayōkam avarkaḷukkut terintatu; vilaiyuyarnta vayiram mutaliya kaṟkaḷil vicittiramāy eḻuttukkaḷ eḻutuvatil tērntiruntārkaḷ; ulōkaṅkaḷil patippittal, iṉāmal pūcutal maṟṟa ulōkaṅkaḷai mēṟ pūcutal mutaliya vēlaikaḷai aṟintiruntārkaḷ; pōr cilēṉ kōppaikaḷ, kaṇṇāṭi karṇakkaṇṇāṭi mutaliyavaṟṟāl pāttiraṅkaḷ mutaliya ceytalum, leṉs kaṇṇāṭiyum avarkaḷukkut terintiruntatu; palavitamāṉa jāṭikaḷ, taṭṭukaḷ, veṇkalam tantam mutaliyavaṟṟāl ceyta āparaṇaṅkaḷ, maṇikaḷ, poṉṉāṟ ceyta kātaṇikaḷ, vicittiramāṉa uruvamum vēlaippāṭumuḷḷa kaikkāppukaḷ mutaliyavaikaḷai avarkaḷ upayōkittu vantārkaḷ.”

“On the north side of the chamber were two doorways leading into separate apartments. Entrance was formed by two colossal bas-reliefs of Dagon, or the fish god. Unfortunately the upper part of all these figures had been destroyed, but as the lower remained from above the waist we can have no difficulty in restoring the whole, especially as the same image is seen entire on a fine Assyrian cylinder of a gate in my possession. It combined the human shape with that of the fish. The head of the fish formed a mitre above that of the man. whilst its scaly back and fanlike tail fell as a cloak behind, leaving the two human limbs and feet exposed. The figure wore a fringed tunic, and bore the two sacred emblems, the basket and the cone.
We can scarcely hesitate to identify this mythic form with the Oannes, or sacred manfish, who according to the traditions preserved by Berossus, issued from the Erythraean  sea, instructed the Chaldaeans in all wisdom, in the sciences, and in the fine arts, and was afterwards whorshipped as a God in the temples of Babylonia. Its body, says the historian, was that of a fish but under the head of a fish was that of a man and to its tail were joined women’s feet. Five such monsters rose from the Persian gulf at fabulous intervals of time. It was conjectured that this myth denotes the conquest of Chaldaea at some remote and prehistoric period, by a comparatively civilised nation coming in ships to the mouth of the Euphrates.
I had already identified with the Babylonian idol a figure in a bas-relief at Khorsabad having the human form to the waist, and the estremities of a fish. Such figures are also frequently found on antique cylinders and gems, but those at Kouyunjik agreed even more minutely with the description of Berossus, for the human head was actually beneath that of the fish whilst the human feet were added to the spreading tail.”
“anta aṟaiyiṉ vaṭappakkattil taṉittaṉi aṟaikaḷukkuc cellum iraṇaṭu vācaṟ katavukaḷ iruntaṉa. ovvoru vācalilum tākōṉ allatu mīṉ teyvattiṉ iraṇṭu piramāṇṭamāṉa uruvaṅkaḷ niṉṟaṉa. āṉāl avvuruvaṅkaḷiṉ mēṟ pākaṅkaḷ aḻintu pōṉatu mikavum vicaṉikkappaṭattakkatu. eṉṟālum avaikaḷiṉ kīḻ pākaṅkaḷ iṭuppu varaiyilum keṭāmal irunta paṭiyālum atē uruvam eṉ vacattiluḷḷa ācīriyāvaic cērnta ciliṇṭar vaṭivamāṉa oru vācaṟpaṭiyil muḻumaiyu māyk kāṇappaṭuvatālum anta muḻu uruvamum eppaṭi yirukkum eṉṟu niccayippatu acāttiyamāṉa kāriyamalla. atu maṉita uruvamum mīṉ uruvamum kalantatu. maṉitaṉuṭaiya talaikku mēl mīṉiṉ uruvamāṉatu oru kirīṭam pōl iruntatu. cetilkaḷ niṟainta ataṉ mutukum viciṟi pōṉṟa vālum oru nilaiyaṅkipōl piṉṉāl viḻuntiruntatu. maṉitak kaikaḷum kālkaḷum pātaṅkaḷum muṉṉē naṉṟāyk kāṇappaṭṭaṉa. cuṟṟilum curukkaṅkaḷuḷḷa oru mēl vastiram atiṉ mēl pōṭap paṭṭiruntatu. paricuttattukku aṭaiyāḷamākiya kūṭaiyum Cone um ataṉ kaiyil iruntaṉa.”

“Lastly come the Inflectional Languages represented by the two groups of the Semetic and Indo-Germanic languages. It is from the speakers of languages of these two groups that almost everything most beneficial to the development of the human race has sprung. The Semetic languages are (a) Hebrew closely akin to which were the other ancient dialects of Canaan, Moabite, Phoenician etc. (b) Arabic, widely spread as the result of Mohamadan Conquests; (c) Aramaic, the languages of Ancient Syria which in Palestine also had taken the place of Hebrew as a spoken language before the Christian era; and (d) Assyrian, which has been recovered from countless inscriptions upon clay tablets found on the sites of ancient cities like Nineveh and Babylon. The different Semetic languages do not differ more from one another than do Romance languages like French, Italian and Spanish. They are, however, generally divided into a northern and a Southern group; the Souhern group being formed of the various dialects of Arabic, the northern groups of the other languages though Aramaic deviates considerably from the rest of the group. The most characteristic feature of the Simitic languages is that with rare exceptions all roots have three Consonants or semi Consonants, which in combination with vowels, form series of words. The verb system is much less perfectly developed than that of the Indo-Germanic system.
To the Indo-Germanic or Indo-European system belong a number of languages and dialects which fall easily into eight groups. These languages are widely spread, extending from India to Iceland in the Old world, and since the end of the fifteenth century having been disseminated over the whole of America, Australia, New Zealand, and the East India as the language of European conquerors or colonizers of those lands. The sysem has been called by other names as Aryan, which is however, more appropriately applied to the most easterly group of the languages. The name Indo-European is commonly used, but seems to imply that the languages are spoken only in India and Europe, which is inaccurate, as is also the notion that all Indian and European languages belong to this system. In Southern Indian the Dravidian languages, of which the chief representatives are Tamil and Telugu are aggultinative languages and therefore of a different type, while in Europe, Turkish, Hungarian, Finnish, Lapp belong to an aggultinative system, and Basque, as we have seen, is an incorporating language. The names Indo-Germanic and Celt-Indic are each an attempt to express the family by the exterme links of the chain. The languages belonging tothe system are descended from an original language long since lost. Where this language was spoken it is difficult definitely to decide.”
kaṭaiciyāka cemiṟṟik intu jermaṉik pāṣaiḷāl kuṟikkappaṭṭa pala vita māṟutalkaḷuḷḷa (Inflexional) pāṣaikaḷ varukiṉṟaṉa. māṉiṭa jāti nākarīka mutaliyavaṟṟil tērcciyaṭaivataṟku evai avaciyamō avai inta iraṇṭu jāti pāṣaikaḷaiyum pēcuvōrālēyē uṇṭāṉavai. cemiṟṟik jātiyaic cērnta pāṣaiḷ evaiyeṉṟāl, (ya) epirēyupāṣai. ātiyil kāṉāṉiyar, mōvāpiyar, peṉikkēyar mutaliyavarkaḷ pēciṉa pāṣaikaḷ itaṟku neruṅkiya campanta muṭaiyavai. (b) arapippāṣai. itu makamatiyaruṭaiya veṟṟikaḷāl anēka tēcaṅkaḷil paraviṉatu (c) aramēyik pāṣaikaḷ. ātiyil cīriyā nāṭṭil pēcappaṭṭa pāṣaikaḷ ivaikaḷē. inta pāṣai kiṟistuvukku muṉ palastīṉā nāṭṭil epirēyu pāṣaikkup patilāy pēcappaṭum oru pāṣaiyāy iruntatu. (d) acīriyapāṣai. niṉivē, pāpilōṉ, mutaliya āti nakaraṅkaḷil veṭṭi yeṭukkappaṭṭa kaḷimaṇ palakaikaḷil kāṇappaṭṭa anēka eḻuttukkaḷāl tāṉ intap pāṣai aḻintu pōkāmal taṟkākkappaṭṭatu. rōmaṉs pāṣaiḷākiya pirañci, ittāliya pāṣai, spāṉiya pāṣai eppaṭi oṉṟaṟkoṉṟu atika vittiyāca millāmal irukkiṉṟaṉavō appaṭiyē cemiṟṟik pāṣaiyaic cērnta paṟpala pāṣaikaḷum oṉṟaṟkoṉṟu atika vittiyācamillāmal irukkiṉṟaṉa. āṉāl avaikaḷ vaṭakku, teṟku eṉṟa iru kūṭṭaṅkaḷāka cātāraṇamāyp pirikkappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. arapip pāṣaiyaic cērnta kiḷai pāṣaikaḷ teṉ kūṭṭattaiyum, maṟṟa pāṣaikaḷ vaṭa kūṭṭattaiyum cērntavai. āṉāl aramēyik pāṣaikkum antak kūṭṭattaic cērnta itara pāṣaikaḷukkum aṉanta vittiyācaṅkaḷ uṇṭu. cemiṟṟik pāṣaikaḷiṉ mukkiyamāṉa aṟikuṟi yeṉṉa veṉṟāl, anēkamāy vārttaikaḷiṉ aṭippakutikaḷellām mūṉṟu uyir mey yeḻuttukaḷ allatu Semi consonants uḷḷavaikaḷāyirukkum. ivaikaḷum uyireḻuttu kaḷum oṉṟu cērumpoḻutu tokutiyāṉa anēka vārttaikaḷ avai kaḷiṉiṉṟu piṟakkum. āṉāl atiṉ viṉaiccol muṟai intu jermāṉik pāṣaikaḷiṉ muṟaiyaip pōla avvaḷavu pūraṇattiṟku vantatalla.
intu jermāṉik allatu intu airōppiyaṉ kūṭṭattaic cērnta pāṣaikaḷaik kavaṉittāl avaikaḷiṉ uṭpirivukaḷāka anēkam perum pāṣaikaḷum pēcappaṭum pāṣaikaḷum irukkiṉṟaṉa. ivaikaḷai mukkiyamāṉa eṭṭuk kūṭṭaṅkaḷāyp pirikkalām. intap pāṣaikaḷ veku vistāramāy ulakattil anēka iṭaṅkaḷil pēcappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. paḻaiya ulakattil avaikaḷ intiyā tēca mutal aislāntu, tēcam varaikkum paḻakkattil irukkiṉṟaṉa. putiya ulakattil 15-m nūṟṟāṇṭiṟkup piṟaku amerikkā, āstirēliyā, nīyūcilāntu, kīḻintiyat tīvukaḷ mutaliya tēcaṅkaḷil avaikaḷai jeyittavarḷuṭaiya pāṣaikaḷākavum allatu avaikaḷil kuṭiyēṟiṉarvaḷuṭaiya pāṣaikaḷākavum iruntu varukiṉṟaṉa. intap pāṣaikaḷukku āriyapāṣaikaḷ eṉṟa maṟu peyarum uṇṭu. āṉāl kīḻakkaṭaiciyil pēcappaṭum pāṣaikaḷukkuttāṉ intap peyar takum. intu airōppiyaṉ eṉum peyar cātāraṇa vaḻakkattilirunta pōtilum, peyaraik koṇṭu atu intiyā airōppā kaṇṭaṅkaḷil pēcappaṭum pāṣai yeṉṟu colvatu tappāṉa apippirāyam. intiyāvilum airōppāvilum vaḻaṅki varum pāṣaikaḷ intak kūṭṭattaic cērntavai yeṉṟu colvatum tappu. teṉṉintiyāvil tamiḻ teluṅku pāṣaikaḷāl kuṟikkappaṭṭa tirāviṭa pāṣaikaḷāṉavai vārttaikaḷaic caṅkilipōl toṭukkum (agglutinative) iṉattaic cērntatāl vittiyācamāṉavai. āṉāl airōppāvilō turukki, haṅkēriya, piṉṉiṣ (Finnish)) lāplāntu tēca pāṣaikaḷ vārttaikaḷaic caṅkilipōl toṭukkum jātiyaic cērntavai. nām munti kavaṉittapaṭi pāskpāṣai maṟṟa pāṣai vārttaiḷait taṉṉuṭaṉ kalakkum (incorporating language) jātiyaic cērntatu. intu jermāṉik, kelṭ intik eṉṉum peyarkaḷ, oru caṅkiliyiṉ antattaiyum ātiyaiyum māttiram eṭuttuk koṇṭu appeyarḷai caṅkili muḻuvatukkum vaittatu pōl irukkiṉṟaṉa. ikkūṭṭattaic cērnta pāṣaikaḷ cantēkamaṉṉiyil orukālam iruntu ippōtu aḻintu pōṉa oru āti pāṣaiyiṉiṉṟu uṟpattiyāyirukka vēṇṭum. āṉāl appērppaṭṭa ātipāṣaiyāṉatu evviṭattil pēcappapaṭṭateṉṟu tīrmāṉippatu ilēcāṉa kāriyamalla.
pāṣaikaḷaip paṟṟit teḷivāṉa apippirāyamum kālamum colvatu ilēcāṉa kāriyamalla. nammuṭaiya kālattil allatu namakkuc camīpa kālattil uṇṭāṉa tiruttam aṭainta pāṣaiyaip paṟṟiyum nūtaṉamāy eḻuttukaḷ uṇṭākkappaṭṭa pāṣaiyaip paṟṟiyum māttiram nām collak kūṭiyatēyoḻiya mikappūrvamāṉa pāṣaiḷaip paṟṟit teḷivāka oṉṟum collakkūṭāta iyalpuṭaiyatāyirukkiṟatu. tamiḻiṉ vārttai kaḷaiyum tamiḻiṉ eḻuttukkaḷaiyum mikavum ottirukkum tamiḻ nāṭṭiṟkuc camīpattiluḷḷa tiruvāṅkūr nāṭṭil pēcappaṭum malaiyāḷa pāṣaiyum teluṅku pāṣaiyum veku camīpa kālattil camaskiruta pāṣaiyiṉ pala eḻuttukkaḷaiyum vārttaikaḷaiyum cērttuk koṇṭu oru periya māṟutalai aṭaintirukkiṉṟaṉa. caurāṣṭira pāṣai (paṭṭu nūṟkārar pāṣai) veku camīpattil eḻutuvataṟkuriya eḻuttu kaṇṭu piṭikkappaṭṭu eḻutum pāṣaiyāyiṟṟu eṉpatai nām aṟivōm. oṉṟaip pārttu oṉṟu tērcciyaṭaivatu ulaka iyalputāṉē. pirakūyis pāṣai yilum cumēriya pāṣaiyilum pala pirākiruta pāṣaikaḷilum pāli pāṣai yilum intu jermāṉik pāṣaikaḷilumuḷḷa pala vārttaikaḷaiyum pala ilakkaṇaṅkaḷaiyum nūtaṉamāṉa cila vitiḷaiyumuṭaiyatāyc cila āyira varuṭaṅkaḷukku muṉṉāka camaskirutam uṇṭāṉateṉṟu itaṉ muṉ pārttirukkiṟōm. camaskiruta pāṣaiyiliruntu cila eḻuttukḷaiyum vārttaikaḷaiyum iraval vāṅkik koṇṭa pāṣaikaḷ iṉṉum āyira varuṭaṅkaḷukkup piṉ camaskirutattiṉiṉṟē uṇṭāyiṉa eṉṟu colla iṭamākumē.
paricuttamāka vāṉattiliruntu viḻum maḻai jalam vāykkālilum, vāykkāliluḷḷatu kuḷattilum, kuḷattiluḷḷa jalam vayalilum, maṟupaṭi avai āṟṟilum, āṟṟi nīr kaṭalilum pāyntu vevvēṟu ruciyaiyum maṇattaiyum niṟattaiyum aṭaivatu eppaṭiyō apṭiyē pāṣaiyiṉ vārttaikaḷum vevvēṟu uccarippum eḻuttukkaḷumuṭaiyavaikaḷāy māṟutalkaḷaṭaivataṟku utāraṇaṅkaḷ itaṉmuṉ colliyirukkiṟōm. ataṟkiṇaṅka ātiyil pala iṭaṅkaḷukkuppōyk kuṭiyēṟiṉa jaṉaṅkaḷ pūrvīkamāyp pēci vanta pāṣai antanta tēcattiṉ cītōṣṇattiṟkut takuntapaṭi upayōkikkum vastiram poruḷkaḷ, viḷaiyum kāy, kaṉi, kīrai mutaliya patārttaṅkaḷukkum niracavastukkaḷukkum paḻakka vaḻakkaṅkaḷukkum takuntavitamāy eḻuttukkaḷum vārttaikaḷum vaṭivamum kālakkiramattil māṟupaṭṭu vēṟu pāṣaiyāyt tōṉṟukiṟatu. ippaṭik koñcam koñca māka māṟutalkaḷaiyuṭaiya pala pāṣaikaḷ akaṇṭamāyirunta pūmi pala aracarkaḷāl vevvēṟāka āḷappaṭumpoḻutu vevvēṟu tēcamākavum vevvēṟu pāṣaiyākavum vevvēṟu tiruttaṅkaḷuṭaiyatākavum ceyyap paṭumpoḻutu muṟṟilum tāyp pāṣaikku ovvātatākak kāṇappaṭu kiṉṟaṉa.
pala carakkukkaṭaiyil cintum navatāṉiyaṅkaḷum pala poruḷkaḷum oṉṟāyk kalanta piṉ piritteṭuppatu kaṣṭamākiṟatu eppaṭiyō, taṅkam veḷḷi vēlai ceyyum taṭṭāṉ kuppaiyiṟ kalanta taṅkattaip pirit teṭuppataṟku taṅkam, veḷḷi, cempu, īyam mutaliya ulōkaṅḷai taṉṉōṭu cērttuk koḷḷum pātaracattiṉāl mutal mutal piritteṭuttu ataṉ piṉ taṅkattaiyum veḷḷiyaiyum māttiram pirikkakkūṭiya cuṇṇāmpuk kukaiyil vaittu ūti ataṉpiṉ veḷḷiyaip pirittu viṭakkūṭiya puṭattiṉāl cutta taṅkattai eṭuppatu evvaḷavu pirayācaiyō atu pōla ituvumirukkiṟatu. pūmiyil putaintu kiṭakkum pūrva ciṉṉaṅkaḷaiyum pāṣaikaḷaip paṟṟiya kuṟippukaḷaiyum ārāyntu eṭukkum carittira ārāyccikkārarukkup pāṣaiyiṉ kalappu mutaliyavai kaḷaip paṟṟic colluvatu piriyamāyirukkumēyoḻiya maṟṟavarukku itu piriyamāyirātu.
“āti tirāviṭaruṭaiya nākarīkamum avarkaḷ nilaimaiyum iṉṉa teṉṟu pūrṇamāy veḷippaṭum kālattil mecōppottāmi yaruṭaiya viruttiyāṉa nākarīkam tirāviṭa tēcattiliruntu aṅku kuṭiyēṟiṉa cumēri yāvil uṇṭāṉa teṉṟu yāvarum oppuk koḷvatu pōlavē vāṉa cāstiramum āti pāṣaiyiṉ eḻuttukkaḷ mutaliya nākarīka ciṉṉaṅkaḷum intiyāvil mutal mutal ārampamāṉateṉṟu oppuk koḷḷappaṭum. āṉāl taṟkāla carittira ārāycciyaik kavaṉikkum poḻutu āti ulaka māṉatu tirāviṭa jātiyārukku ivvaḷavu tūram kaṭamaippaṭṭiruntatu eṉṟa caṅkatiyaip pūrva intiyāvaip paṟṟip pēcum taṟkāla carittirakkārar eṭuttuc collakkūṭa māṭṭārkaḷ” eṉṟu 184m pakkattil Mr. A. Ghose eṉpavar eḻutiya kuṟippukaḷai nām pārkkum poḻutu avai uṇmai yākavē tōṉṟukiṉṟaṉa. ātaliṉāl ivviṣayattaip paṟṟic cila vārttaikaḷ collat tuṇintēṉ.
intiyāviṉ teṉpuṟattilinta vicālamāṉa nāṭu tamiḻ nāṭāyirunta teṉṟum pāṇṭiya rājarkaḷāl āḷappaṭṭateṉṟum, iyal icai nāṭaka meṉṉum muttamiḻum aṅkē viruttiyaṭainta teṉṟum avaṟṟil icait tamiḻil vīcam curam varaikkum nuṭpamāṉa curaṅkaḷil kāṉam ceytārka ḷeṉṟum itaṉmuṉ pārttirukkiṟōm. atupōlavē iyaṟṟamiḻil iyaṟkai amaippil kāṇappaṭum ceyalkaḷaiyum jīvap pirāṇikaḷiṉ ōcaiyaiyu muṭaiyatāyp pala aruṅkalaikaḷilum tērnta tāyiruntatu tamiḻ moḻiyeṉṟu pala tiṣṭāntaṅkaḷiṉāl colliyirukkiṟōm.
iṅkē intu jermāṉik eṉṟa pāṣaiyum cemiṟṟik pāṣaiyumāka iraṇṭu pirivukaḷil pāṣaikaḷ uṇṭāyirukkalāmeṉṟu collukiṟār. cemiṟṟik pāṣai eṉpatu ēpirēyupāṣai, arapi pāṣai, aramēyik pāṣai, acīriya pāṣai eṉṟu vakukkappaṭṭirukkiṟatu. intu jermāṉik pāṣai eṉpatu paḻaiya ulakattil intiyā tēcam mutal iṅkilāntiṟku vaṭakkēyuḷḷa aislāntu tīvu varai paḻakkattilirunta pala pāṣaikaḷākavum avaṟṟiṉ uṭpirivukaḷākavum terikiṟatu.
atu patiṉaintām nūṟṟāṇṭiṟkup piṟaku amērikkā, āstirēliyā, niyucilāntu, kīḻ intiya tīvukaḷ mutaliya tēcaṅkaḷil pēcappaṭum pāṣai kaḷākavumirukkiṟatu. intu airōppiya pāṣai eṉṟu collumpoḻutu intiyā airōppā kaṇṭaṅkaḷil pēcappaṭum pāṣai eṉṟu nām niṉaikkak kūṭāteṉṟum intu pāṣaiyeṉṟu collumpoḻutu tamiḻ, teluṅku eṉṟu māttiram niṉaikkappaṭāteṉṟum collukiṟār. āṉāl intiyā mutal aislāntu uḷpaṭa ettaṉai tēcaṅkaḷ aṭaṅki irukkiṉṟaṉavō atupōlavē intu pāṣai ātiyāka jermaṉ pāṣai yīṟākavuḷḷa pala pāṣaikaḷum itil aṭaṅkum. oru caṅkiliyiṉ iru kaṭaiciyiluḷḷa vaḷaiyaṅkaḷaik kuṟippiṭṭatupōl iṅkēyum kuṟippiṭṭirukkiṟatāka nām niṉaikka vēṇṭum. intu, jermāṉik, kelṭ intik mutaliyavaikaḷaip pōl collappaṭukiṟatu eṉṟu nām aṟiya vēṇṭum. ikkūṭṭattiluḷḷa pāṣaikaḷ pala aḻintu pōyiṉaveṉṟum pala pāṣaikaḷiṉ kalappiṉāl ātipāṣai iṉṉateṉṟum atilintu maṟṟa pāṣaikaḷ uṟpattiyāṉa vitam iṉṉateṉṟum evviṭattil pēcappaṭṭateṉṟum tīrmāṉippatu lēcāṉa kāriyamallaveṉṟum collukiṟār.
itai nām kavaṉikkaiyil cemiṟṟik pāṣaiyiliruntu uṇṭāṉa epirēyu pāṣaiyil cātāraṇa tamiḻ moḻikaḷ atikam kalantiruppataik koṇṭum epirēyu pāṣaiyiṉ vārttai tamiḻil kalavātiruppataik koṇṭu epirēyu pāṣaikkum tamiḻ moḻi muntiṉateṉṟu terikiṟatu. epirēyu pāṣaikkut tāyaṉa cemiṟṟik pāṣaiyilum tamiḻmoḻi kalantirukka vēṇṭum. cemiṟṟik pāṣaikkum tamiḻ moḻi muntiṉatā yirukka vēṇṭum. aramēyik pāṣai epirēyupāṣaikkup piṟaku kiṟistu vukku muṉ palastīṉā nāṭṭil pēcappaṭṭateṉṟu collukiṟatiṉāl tamiḻ kalanta epirēyupāṣaiyum atil kalantirukka vēṇṭum.
acīriyapāṣai niṉivē pāpilōṉ mutaliya nakaraṅkaḷil vaḻaṅki vanta teṉṟum appāṣaiyil eḻutappaṭṭa maṇ ōṭukaḷ putainta nakaraṅkaḷil kāṇappaṭukiṉṟaṉaveṉṟum appāṣaiyiṉ pala eḻuttukkaḷiṉ ōcai tamiḻp pāṣaiyiṉ eḻuttukkaḷiṉ ōcaiyākavēyirukkiṟa teṉṟum cumēriyar ippaṭṭaṇaṅkaḷaik kaṭṭiṉārkaḷ eṉṟum, aracāṭci ceytārka ḷeṉṟum cumēriyar tirāviṭarkaḷā yiruntārkaḷeṉṟum, intiyāviṉ teṉpākattiliruntu aṅkuk kuṭiyēṟiṉārkaḷeṉṟum, kaltēyarukku muṉṉāl pūrvam oru palatta jātiyār aṅkē yiruntu aracāṭci ceytārkaḷeṉṟum, avarkaḷ kappal mūlamākap pāracīkakkuṭāviṉ vaḻiyāy vantārkaḷ eṉṟum, avarkaḷ mīṉ uruvamāṉa teyvattai vaṇaṅki vantārkaḷeṉṟum, vilai uyarnta vayiram, cikappu mutaliya kaṟkaḷil mīṉ vaṭivam kāṇappaṭṭateṉṟum, colvataik kavaṉikkaiyil iṉṉa kālameṉṟu niccayam colla muṭiyāta pūrvakālattil tamiḻ makkaḷ mecōppottāmiyā nāṭṭilum ataic cuṟṟilumuḷḷa pāracīkam, pelujistāṉ mutaliya nāṭukaḷilum kuṭiyēṟiṉārkaḷeṉṟum, aracāṭci ceytārkaḷeṉṟum avarkaḷ pāṣaiyē pakkattu nāṭukaḷilum pala pētaṅkaḷaiyaṭaintu vaḻaṅki vanta teṉṟum eṇṇa iṭamirukkiṟatu. itōṭu intu jermāṉik pāṣaiyaiyum ataṉ kiḷaip pāṣaikaḷaiyum kavaṉittāl tamiḻ vārttaikaḷ ērāḷamāka avaṟṟil kalantiruppataik kāṇalām.
airōppiya pāṣaiyil kāṇappaṭum tamiḻ vārttaikaḷukku utāraṇamāka 100 vārttaikaḷ muṉpu colliyirukkiṟōm. ivvārttai kaḷaik kavaṉippōmāṉāl tamiḻ nāṭṭiṉ jaṉaṅkaḷ paḻakkattil cātāraṇamāka upayōkikkum tamiḻ moḻikaḷāyirukkiṉṟaṉaveṉṟu nām aṟivōm. āṉāl jermāṉik allatu airōppiyaṉ kūṭṭattaic cērnta pala pāṣaikaḷiṉ vārttaikaḷil ētāvatu oṉṟu intiya pāṣaiyil (tamiḻ moḻiyil) kalavātu pallāyira varuṭaṅkaḷukku muṉpē taṉitta ciṟappuṟṟatāyp pōtumāṉa ilakkaṇa ilakkiyaṅkaḷuṭaiyatāyt tērnta kalaikaḷuṭaiyatāyc caṅkītattil nāḷatu varaiyum maṟṟavarkaḷāl kaṇṭu piṭikkappaṭāta nuṭpamāṉa pākupāṭukaḷai yuṭaiyatāyiruppataik kavaṉittāl intiyāvil oru kālam mikuntu vaḻaṅki vanta tamiḻ moḻiyē pūrvamāṉa moḻi eṉṟu colla niyāyamirukkiṟatu.
oru caṅkiliyiṉ ātiyum antamumāṉa iraṇṭu vaḷaiyaṅkaḷaip pōl intu jermāṉik pāṣaiyiruppatāl itaṉ naṭuvil oṉṟō ṭoṉṟu campantappaṭṭa pala vaḷaiyaṅkaḷiruppatu pōl intu pāṣai mutal jermāṉik pāṣai varaiyum pala kalappuṟṟa pāṣaikaḷ vaḻaṅki yirukka vēṇṭumeṉpatu uṇmaiyē.
intiyā mutal ettiyōppiyā tēcam varaiyumuḷḷa 127 tēcaṅkaḷai yum āṇṭu koṇṭirunta ākāsvēruviṉ rājyattaik kavaṉippō māṉāl taṉatu cūcāṉ paṭṭaṇattil 127 tēcaṅkaḷiluḷḷa irājarkaḷukkum, pirapukkaḷukkum āṟumātam viruntu ceytāṉ eṉṟu collappaṭukiṟatu. atōṭu cumēriyar pāpilōṉ niṉivē mutaliya iṭaṅkaḷilum aracāṭci ceytu vantārkaḷ. avarkaḷ tamiḻ nāṭṭiliruntupōṉa tamiḻ makkaḷ pāracīkattilum, pelujistāṉ malaikaḷilum kuṭiyiruntavarkaḷ pēciya pirakūyis pāṣaiyaik kavaṉikkumpoḻutum avarkaḷum tamiḻarkaḷākavē yiruntārkaḷ. kaltēyarukku muṉṉirunta pūrva kuṭikaḷ vaṇaṅki vanta mīṉ corupa (tākōṉ vikkiraka)ttaik koṇṭum, pacuvaik koṇṭum avarkaḷum tamiḻ makkaḷāyirukka vēṇṭum.
cattiyavētattil collappaṭukiṟa tākōṉ eṉṉum vikkirakam mīṉ vaṭivamāyiruntateṉṟum pelistar atai vaṇaṅkiṉārkaḷeṉṟum piṉvarum varikaḷāl kāṇalām.
cattiya vētam ai cāmuvēl 5-2.
“pelistar tēvaṉuṭaiya peṭṭiyaip piṭittu tākōṉiṉ kōvililē koṇṭu vantu tākōṉaṇṭaiyilē vaittārkaḷ.”
cattiya vētam niyāyātipatikaḷ 16-23.
“pelistariṉ pirapukkaḷ nammuṭaiya pakaiñaṉākiya cimcōṉai nammuṭaiya tēvaṉ nammuṭaiya kaiyil oppuk koṭuttār eṉṟu colli taṅkaḷ tēvaṉākiya tākōṉukku oru periya pali celuttavum cantōṣam koṇṭāṭavum kūṭivantārkaḷ.”
Biblical Cyclopaedia Page 190.
“Dagon. (1 Sam. V. 2). This was the name of a celebrated idol of the Philistines, worshipped at Gaza, (Judg. XVI. 23) at Ashdod, (1 Sam. V.1.3) at Beth dagon, (“the house or temple of Dagon”) in the bounds of Judah, (Josh XV. 41) in a town of Asher, (Josh XIX. 27) and elsewhere. There are various opinions as to the appearance of this idol, but it is usually represented with the head, hands, and face of a man, and the body like that of a fish. The name was probably derived from dag signifying a large fish. One of the incarnations of the Hindu god Vishnu was of the same form.”
“tākōṉ (1 cāmu. 5.2.) yūtēyā tēcattil uḷḷa (yōcu 15.41) ācēr (yōcu 19.27) eṉṉum nakarilum maṟṟum iṭaṅkaḷilum, kācā (niyā 16.23) astōt (1 cāmu. 5.1-3) pettākōṉ (tākōṉuṭaiya vīṭu kōyil) eṉṉum iṭaṅkaḷilum vaṇaṅkappaṭṭa oru pērpōṉa vikkirakattiṉ peyar. anta vikkirakattiṉ uruvattaip paṟṟip pala apippirāyaṅkaḷ irunta pōtilum, cātāraṇamāy atu maṉita talai, mukam, kaikaḷuṭaiyatākavum, mīṉaippōṉṟa uṭal uruvamuṭaiyatāyumiruntatākat terikiṟatu. Dag eṉpataṟku “oru periya mīṉ” eṉṟa arttam iruntatāka ūkikkalām. intukkaḷuṭaiya teyvaṅkaḷil oṉṟākiya viṣṇu mīṉ avatāram eṭuttatākac collappaṭuvataiyum kavaṉikka vēṇṭum.”
mēṟkaṇṭa vacaṉaṅkaḷāl teṉmaturaiyil aracāṇṭukoṇṭirunta cattiya virataṉaip piraḷayattiṉiṉṟum kāppāṟṟa avataritta makāviṣṇu viṉ mīṉ uruvattaip pelistarkaḷum avarkaḷuk karukilirunta ayal nāṭṭārum vaṇaṅki vantirukkiṟārkaḷeṉṟu terikiṟatu. ākaiyāl oru kālattil teṉ pāṇṭi nāṭṭiliruntupōṉa tamiḻarkaḷ mecōpottā miyāvukkup pōy aṅkiruntu pala rājyaṅkaḷaiyum stāpittu pala rājyattārākavum pala tēcattārākavum pala pāṣaikkārarākavum pirintu viruttiyaṭaintiruntārkaḷeṉṟum avarkaḷ pēci vanta pāṣai kālak kiramattil pala pāṣaikaḷāka aḻaikkappaṭiṉum tamiḻmoḻi kalappuṭaiyatā yiṟṟeṉṟum colla ētuvirukkiṟatu. annāṭṭil pala rājyattārukkum potuvāka mīṉ corūpam teyvamāyiruntatu pōlat tamiḻ moḻiyē potuvāṉa moḻiyāyiruntirukka vēṇṭum.
camaskirutattil vaḻaṅki varum tamiḻ vārttaikaḷaiyum camas kirutattiṟkum, tamiḻukkum potuvāṉateṉṟu collappaṭum tamiḻ vārttaikaḷaiyum, airōppiya pāṣaikaḷil kāṇappaṭum tamiḻ vārttai kaḷaiyum, cīttiyapāṣaiyil kāṇappaṭum tamiḻ vārttaikaḷaiyum muṉpu utāraṇamākak kāṭṭiyirukkiṟōm.
camaskiruta moḻikaḷum, airōppiya moḻikaḷum, cīttiya moḻikaḷum tamiḻ moḻiyōṭu kalantiruppatāka 2000 varuṭaṅkaḷukku muṉṉuḷḷa tamiḻ nūlkaḷil kāṇamāṭṭōm. itaṉālēyē tamiḻmoḻi ātiyil uṇṭāṉa teṉṟum avaṟṟil iyal icai nāṭakameṉṉum muttamiḻum pōtumāṉa tērcci peṟṟiruntateṉṟum avaṟṟil icaittamiḻākiya caṅkītam mikavum naṉṟāka oḻuṅkupaṭuttappaṭṭu maṉatil tōṉṟum karuttukaḷattaṉaiyum koṇṭatāṉa irāka amaippuṭaiya tāyiruntateṉṟum teḷivāyt terikiṟatu.
atōṭu vālillāk kuraṅkukaḷ varicaiyāyppāṭum paṉṉiru curaṅkaḷē āyappālaiyiṉ paṉṉiru curaṅkaḷāka eṭuttuk koṇṭiruppataik koṇṭu itu maṉita uṟpattiyiṉ kāla mutal tamiḻ nāṭṭiliruntu viruttiyāṉa teṉṟu eṇṇa iṭamirukkiṟatu. pāṣaiyiṉ ārampattaiyum caṅkītattiṉ ārampattaiyum maṟṟum tamiḻ makkaḷ vaḻaṅki vanta kalaikaḷiṉ uṭkaruttaiyum oṉṟu cērttup pārttāl tamiḻ moḻiyiṉ pūrvīkattaiyum icait tamiḻiṉ (caṅkītattiṉ) nuṭpattaiyum iṉimai yaiyum evar kaṇṭu collak kūṭiyavar?
oru stāyiyaip paṉṉiraṇṭāyp pirippatil 2/3, 3/4 muṟaiyil kiṭaikkum 2/3, 3/4, 4/5, 5/6, 3/5, 5/8 mutaliya curaṅkaḷiṉ oṟṟumai yillāmaiyai nām kavaṉikkumpoḻutu, ca-pa muṟaiyil iṇai iṇaiyāy ēḻāvatu. ēḻāvatu irāciyāy ca-ma vāka kiḷai kiḷaiyāy aintāvatu aintāvatu irāciyāyk kaṇṭupiṭittirunta pūrva tamiḻ makkaḷiṉ āyappālaiyākiya mutalpaṭikkē iṉṉum maṟṟa tēcattavar vantu eṭṭa villai eṉpatu teḷivāka irukkiṟatu. atōṭu āyappālaiyāy vaḻaṅki vanta paṉṉiraṇṭu curaṅkaḷum kaṇṭupiṭippatil ca-pavil koñcam koñcam kuṟaittu oru stāyiyaip paṉṉiraṇṭākat tamiḻ makkaḷ muṟaipōl pirittiruntālum cariyāṉa kaṇakkuc collāmaiyiṉāl Equal Temperament muṟaiyeṉṟu ēḷaṉam ceyyappaṭukiṟatēyoḻiya nallateṉṟu koṇṭāṭap paṭavillai.
oru stāyiyai 24 alakukaḷākap pirittut tamiḻ makkaḷ vaḻaṅki vanta vaṭṭappālaiyiṉ irakaciyam teriyāmal oru stāyiyil 22 curutikaḷ varukiṉṟaṉaveṉṟum ammuṟaippaṭi irākaṅkaḷ pāṭappaṭa vēṇṭu meṉṟum, camaskiruta nūlōr iraṇṭāvatu paṭiyilēyē cantēkam koṇṭārkaḷ.
mutaṟ paṭiyaik kāṇāmalum, iraṇṭāvatu paṭiyiṉ cantēkam tīrāmalu mirukkum poḻutu mūṉṟāvatu, nālāvatu tupaṭikaḷaik kēṭpāṉēṉ? āyap pālai, vaṭṭappālai, tirikōṇap pālai, caturap pālaikaḷil vaḻaṅki varum nuṭpa curaṅkaḷaiyum, paṇkaḷaiyum paṭittu aṉupavappaṭṭavarkaḷ tamiḻiṉ pūrvīkattaiyum atil icaittamiḻiṉ uyarvaiyum iṉi oruvāṟu aṟivārkaḷ.
maṉita, miruka, paṭci, ūrvaṉa, tāvaraṅkaḷaiyum pāṭupavaṉ maṉataiyum kēṭpavaṉ maṉacaiyum teyvattaiyum cantōṣappaṭuttumpaṭiyāṉa caṅkītam icait tamiḻil mika nuṭpamāṉa curutiyuṭaṉ paṉṉīrāyiram āti icaikaḷākat tamiḻ makkaḷāl pāṭappaṭṭu vantataiyum maṟṟa tēcattavar paṉṉiraṇṭu curaṅkaḷukkē tiṭṭamāṉa kaṇakkillāmal 2/3, 3/4 aik kūṭṭip perukkik koṇṭiruppataiyum nām kavaṉippōmāṉāl tamiḻ moḻiyē pūrvamāṉa tāy moḻi eṉṟum icait tamiḻē āti caṅkītameṉṟum cantēka maṟat teḷivākak kāṇpōm.



3. karnāṭaka caṅkītattil vaḻaṅki varum curutikaḷaip paṟṟiya muṭivurai.
karuṇāmirta cākarattiṉ ellaiyāy niṉṟa curam, curutikaḷ, nuṭpamāṉa curutikaḷai ituvaraiyum kavaṉittu vantōm. caṅkīta cāstirattiṟku iv viṣayam mika mukkiyamāṉateṉṟu eṇṇukiṟēṉ.
tamiḻp pāṣaikku uyir eḻuttu, meyyeḻuttu, uyirmeyyeḻuttu, āyuta eḻuttum kaṇitattiṟku mēlvāy ilakkaṅkaḷ kīḻvāy ilakkaṅ kaḷum eppaṭi avaciyamāṉatō appaṭiyē caṅkītattil vaḻaṅki varum ōcaikaḷai aṟivataṟku āyappālaiyil vaḻaṅki varum paṉṉiraṇṭāṉa araic curaṅkaḷum, vaṭṭappālaiyil vaḻaṅki varum irupattunālāṉa kāl curaṅkaḷum, tiri kōṇappālaiyil vaḻaṅki varum nāṟpatteṭṭāṉa araikkāl curaṅkaḷum, caturappālaiyil vaḻaṅki varum toṇṇūṟṟāṟāṉa vīcam curaṅkaḷum mika mukkiyamāṉavai. ivaṟṟaip pūrva tamiḻ makkaḷ payiṉṟu vanta yāḻil kamakaṅkaḷāka vaḻaṅki vantirukkiṟārkaḷ. ippoḻutum yāḻ vācippōr vaḻaṅki varukiṟārkaḷ. itaṉ nuṭpam iṉṉateṉṟu teḷivākac collum pūrva tamiḻ nūlkaḷ maṟaintapiṉ “yāṉai kaṇṭa kuruṭareṉa” caṅkītattil vaḻaṅki varum nuṭpamāṉa curaṅkaḷukkup palar palavitamākak kaṇakkuc coṉṉārkaḷ.
atōṭu cumār 2500 varuṭaṅkaḷukkumuṉ intiyāviṟku vantu pōṉavarāṉa paitākōras eṉṉum tattuva ñāṉiyiṉāl ca-pa 2/3, ca-ma 3/4 eṉṟu vīṇait tantiyiṉ aḷavu mēṟṟicaikkuk koṇṭu pōkappaṭṭu atiliruntu palavittiyācamāṉa kaṇakkukaḷ ēṟpaṭṭaṉa.
intiyāvilirunta camaskiruta vittuvāṉkaḷiṟ paratar, caṅkīta ratṉākarar pōṉṟavarkaḷ oru stāyiyil 22 curutikaḷ varukiṉṟaṉaveṉṟu curaṅkaḷukkuc curutiyiṉ kaṇakkum irāka ilakṣaṇamum colli vaittārkaḷ. itaṉāl karnāṭaka caṅkītattilum, maṟṟum caṅkītattilum vaḻaṅki varum curaṅkaḷaiyum, curutikaḷaiyum niccayippatu kūṭāta kāriyamāy muṭintatu.
karnāṭaka caṅkītattil vaḻaṅki varum curam curutikaḷ iṉṉavaiyeṉṟu terintu koṇṭāloḻiya oru irākattai uṇṭākkavum iṉimaiyuṭaṉ pāṭavum kūṭiyatalla veṉpatu niccayam. irākaṅkaḷai uṇṭākkavum, pāṭik koṇṭirukkum irākaṅkaḷiṉ piḻaikaḷait tiruttik koḷḷavum kūṭiyatāṉa oru muṟaiyaik kaṇṭa nāṉ atai caṅkīta vittuva cirō maṇikaḷ yāvarukkum piracittappaṭutti viruttikkuk koṇṭu varuvataṟ kākac caṅkīta vityā makājaṉa caṅkam eṉṟu oru capai 1912 varuṭam mē mātam 27-m tētiyil ēṟpaṭuttiṉēṉ.
atil nāṭṭai irākattil varum curaṅkaḷ iṉṉavaiyeṉṟu capai yōrāl vicārikkappaṭṭatu. eḻupattiraṇṭu mēḷakkarttāviṉpaṭi kuṟikka vēṇṭumeṉṟu cilarum tuvāvimcati curutiyiṉpaṭi kuṟikka vēṇṭumeṉṟu cilarum vātāṭiṉārkaḷ. vīṇaiyil kaṇṭapaṭi kuṟikka vēṇṭumeṉṟu micca māṉavarkaḷ coṉṉālum curam curutikaḷaip paṟṟiya teḷivāṉa apip pirāyam collak kūṭāmaiyiṉāl aṭutta kāṉpareṉsil tīrmāṉippa tākavum apippirāyam collakkūṭiyavarkaḷ colla vēṇṭumeṉṟum kēṭṭuk koḷḷappaṭṭatu. appaṭiyē 6 kāṉpareṉcukaḷilum pūrṇamāy vicārikkappaṭṭatu.
curutikaḷaip paṟṟic coṉṉavarkaḷiṉ kaṇakkum avarkaḷ aṉupava mum oṉṟaṟkoṉṟu ovvāmalum muṉṉukkup piṉ virōtamāyum iruntataṉāl nāṉum curutiyaip paṟṟic cila colla vēṇṭiyatāyiṟṟu. atiṉāl curutikaḷaip paṟṟic collum palaruṭaiya vevvēṟu apip pirāyaṅkaḷaiyum  ellārukkum eṭuttukkāṭṭuvatum tuvāvimcati curuti muṟai karnāṭaka caṅkītattiṟku ottuvarāteṉṟu rucuppaṭuttuvatum avaciya māyiruntatu. intiyāviṉ pūrva kuṭikaḷ vaḻaṅki vanta icaittamiḻiṉ nuṭpam iṉṉateṉṟu vicārippatu mukkiyameṉat tōṟṟiṟṟu.
pūrva tamiḻ makkaḷ vaḻaṅki vanta āyappālai, vaṭṭappālai, tirikōṇappālai, caturappālai eṉṟa nālu pālaikaḷukkum avarkaḷ collum karuttiṉpaṭi aḷavum, kirakam māṟum poḻutu paṉṉiru pālai yuṇṭākum muṟaiyum, avaikaḷil ēḻu perumpālaikaḷaiyum colla nērntatu. ēḻu curaṅkaḷukkum, paṉṉiru araic curaṅkaḷukkum irupattu nāṉku curutikaḷukkum maṟṟum nuṭpamāṉa curutikaḷukkum taṟkālattavar collum ōcaiyiṉ alaikaḷiṉ kaṇakkum ceṉṭs kaṇakkum kāṭṭa vēṇṭiyatāyiṟṟu.
curam curutikaḷaippaṟṟic collum kaṇakkil 2/3, 3/4, 4/5, 5/6 pōṉṟa piṉṉa aḷavuḷḷa cariyāṉa ōcaiyaik koṭukkamāṭṭātākaiyiṉāl pūrva tamiḻ nūliṉ karuttiṉpaṭikkum caṅkīta ratṉākarariṉ karuttiṉpaṭikkum iraṇṭiṟkuriya turuvalakkattaik (Logarithm) koṇṭu curaṅkaḷukkum curutikaḷukkum kaṇakkuk kaṇṭu piṭikkappaṭṭirukkiṟatu. iraṇṭiṟkuriya turuvalakkattiṉpaṭi (Logarithm)  curaṅkaḷukkum curutikaḷukkum kiṭaikkum tantiyiṉ aḷavum atil pēcappaṭum curaṅkaḷum iṉṉavaiyeṉṟu taṉittu aṭṭavaṇaiyākavum koṭukkappaṭṭirukkiṟatu.
av aṭṭavaṇaiyil kaṇṭa curaṅkaḷ taṟkālam karnāṭaka caṅkītattil vaḻaṅki varukiṉṟaṉa eṉpataṟku utāraṇamāka 67 karnāṭaka irākaṅkaḷ nālu aṭṭavaṇaiyāyk kāṭṭappaṭṭirukkiṉṟaṉa.
atōṭu yāvarum aṟintu koḷḷakkūṭiya vitamāka Staff notationil kuṟikkum muṟaiyum mēṟṟicai caṅkītattiṟkum intiya caṅkītattiṟkumuḷḷa cura oṟṟumaiyum teḷivākak kāṭṭiyirukkiṟēṉ. tamiḻnāṭṭil mikap pūrvamāyuḷḷa icaittamiḻaip piṟkālattiya tamiḻ aracarkaḷum mikavum ātarittu vantārkaḷeṉṟu kāṇpataṟkuc cila cācaṉaṅkaḷ kāṭṭap paṭṭirukkiṉṟaṉa.

4. teṉṉintiya caṅkītattil vaḻaṅki varum curutikaḷum parōṭāvil his haiṉas makārājā avarkaḷ naṭattiya All India Music kāṉpareṉsum.
1913-m varuṭam ākasṭu mātam 9-m tētiyil tañcaiyil naṭanta nālāvatu caṅkīta vityā makājaṉa caṅkattiṟkup piraciṭeṉṭāyirukkumpaṭi nāṉ Devan Sahib V.P. mātavarāv avarkaḷai nēril kēṭṭuk koṇṭa poḻutu avarkaḷum cantōṣamāy oppuk koṇṭu akkirācaṉam vakittu capaiyai mika naṉṟāka naṭattiṉārkaḷ. ataṉ piṉ caṅkīta viṣayamāka ippaṭi oru capaiyai nam intiyāviluḷḷa Native  irājākkaḷil oruvar naṭattiṉāl mikap pirayōjaṉamāyirukkum. nam intiya tēca caṅkītam cīrtiruttamaṭaiyum. appaṭi oru kāṉperaṉs naṭaipeṟumāṉāl tāṅkaḷum vantiruntu mukkiyamāṉa kāriyaṅkaḷil utavi ceyya vēṇṭum eṉṟu kēṭṭuk koṇṭārkaḷ. ataṉpiṟaku appaṭiyē his haiṉas parōṭā makārājā avarkaḷukkum apippirāya miruppatākavum 1915-m varuṣam ṭicampar mātam kāṉpareṉs naṭattap pōkiṟatākavum ataṟku nīṅkaḷum varavēṇṭum eṉṟum eṉakku nēril coṉṉārkaḷ. atikak kuḷirāyiruppatiṉāl pepravari kaṭaici allatu mārccu mātattil vaittuk koṇṭāl nāṉ varukiṟataṟku aṉukūlamāyirukkumeṉṟu kēṭṭuk koṇṭēṉ. ataṟ kiṇaṅki makārājā avarkaḷukkum maṟṟum avarkaḷ pirajaikaḷukkum aṉukūlamāṉa kāmaṉ paṇṭikai naṭakkum tiṉaṅkaḷil mārccu mātam 20-m tēti mutal 25-m tēti varaiyum miyūcik kāṉpareṉs naṭattappaṭṭatu.
intiyāviṉ pala pākaṅkaḷil curutiyaip paṟṟiyum caṅkītattiṉ maṟṟum viṣayaṅkaḷaip paṟṟiyum vicārittuk koṇṭirukkum aṟivāḷi kaḷil 23 pērkaḷ memparkaḷākat terinteṭukkappaṭṭatōṭu maṟṟum pala iṭaṅkaḷiliruntum intustāṉi caṅkītam karnāṭaka caṅkītaṅkaḷil tērnta pēr peṟṟa pala vitvāṉkaḷ aḻaikkappaṭṭiruntārkaḷ. evvitamāṉa kuṟaivumiṉṟi ellōrum cantōṣaṅ koṇṭāṭakkūṭiya vitamāyt taṅkuvataṟkum pōjaṉattiṟkum ēṟṟa vacatikaḷum veku vimaricaiyāka ēṟpaṭṭiruntaṉa. annāṭkaḷ irājāṅkattiṟkuriya paṇṭikai nāṭkaḷ āṉatāl varuṭantōṟum iyalpāy naṭakkum uṟcavac ciṟappum caṅkīta kaccērikaḷum irājā piṟanta nāḷ koṇṭāṭṭamum miyūcik kāṉpareṉs naṭakkum capaiyum oṉṟucērntu iravu pakal iṉṉateṉṟu teriyāmal nāḷ muḻuvatum koṇṭāṭappaṭṭatu.
parōṭā tivāṉ cāpi His Excellency V.P.mātavarāv avarkaḷ  ivaikaḷ yāvaṟṟaiyum mēṟpārttuc capaiyai naṭatti vantārkaḷ. tiṅkaṭkiḻamai kālai eṭṭu maṇikku miyūcik kāṉpareṉs capai ārampittatu. cariyāṉa nērattil makārājā avarkaḷum, makārāṇi avarkaḷum, avarkaḷ puttirarum vara capaiyōr ellārum mikavum cantōṣattuṭaṉ vaṇakkam ceytārkaḷ.

The All-India Music Conference, Baroda.
20th March 1916 to 24th March 1916.
PROGRAMME
OPENING OF THE CONFERENCE.
As soon as His Highness the Maharaja Saheb alights, the President, Secretary and Members of Committee will receive him at the steps of the College Hall and conduct the Royal Party to their seats. After they are seated, the Misses Abraham Pandither will recite the verses composed in praise of God from the Platform. A group of school-children will then recite verses in praise of His Highness the Maharaja Saheb.
The Chairman of the Managing Committee will then address His Highness explaining the aims and objects of the Conference, the circumstances under which it was constituted and request His Highness to open the Conference. His Highness will then declare the Conference open.
The Committee will then elect a President for the Conference. The Chairman of the Committee will propose the name of Thakur Nawab Ali of Akbarpur as President of the Conference and Mr. Masani, the Minister of Education will second the proposal. After the President is dule elected, he will take his seat on the dais and the proceedings will then begin as shown below :-

The Bombay Chronicle, 22nd March 1916.
The All-India Music Conference met this morning in the College Hall which was tastefully decorated for the occasion. Their Highness the Maharaja and Maharani Gaekwar, the Princes, Princesses, the maharaja of Kollengode and family, the heads of all the departments and a large number of ladies and gentlemen, many of whom had specially come from distant parts of India.
The members of the Conference included Prince Faluknaz Mahomed Baker Alli Bahadur, Rao Saheb M. Abraham Pandither and daughters. Thakur Nawab Ali Khan of Akbarpur, Atya Begum Fyzee Rahmin, Mr. V.N. Bhatkhande, Rao Bahadur K.B.Dewal, Mr. E.Clements, Messrs. N.B. and K.B.Divatra, Mr. Lakshmidass Aditram, Mr. M.S. Ramaswamy Iyer, Mr. T.A. Ramakrishna Iyer, Mr, Mangesh Rao, R. Telang and others.
The proceedings opened with the daughters of Mr. Abraham Pandither reciting “kirtans”. A group of school children especially trained by Miss Engineer, Principal of the Female Training College, then recited verses in praise of his Highness the Gaekwar.
Baroda’s Lead
Mr. V.P. Madhava Rao, Chairman of the Managing Committee, in requesting his Highness the Maharaja Gaekwar to open the Conference, explained the aims and objects of the Conference, the circumstances under which it was constituted, and said :-
“The idea of systematising Indian music and placing it on a scientific basis with a view to improving it and making it a better expression of the emotions, has been uppermost in Your Highness’s mind for many years. Baroda had the distinction of having patronised the famous musician Moula Bux, who, if I am not mistaken, was among the first in attempting to reduce Indian music to notation. Latterly, the necessity of notation has been pressed on Your Highness’s attention by music being made one of the subjects of study in the schools of the State, and since the introduction of mass education in regard to which Baroda has the distinction of taking the lead a further emphasis has been laid on this need for notation.
I well remember how interested Your Highness was whenever you hear of Conference for improving Indian music being held during your recent tour in South India. The Conference which Your Highness is going to open is no ordinary event in the annals of the State. Ever sincere the disappearance of Hindu and Mahomedan kingdoms in India, the science and art of music have fallen into a decadent condition and only those that have read the letters from the various correspondents in different parts of India can realise the enthusiasm that prevails everywhere regarding the Conference and how it is looked upon as an epoch-making event in the history of India.
Many of those who have honoured us with their presence at this Conference have devoted their whole life time and almost all their resources to research work and their joy is unbounded to see that through the enlightened liberality and munificence of Your Highness they have been afforded an opportunity of bringing their labours to be tested and valued by such a competent body of experts.
I shall not take up Your Highness’s time by dwelling on the merits of the members who have responded to our call, but it may be permissible for me to point out the valuable acquisition we have in the person of Thakur Nawab Ali of Akbarpur, Mr. Clements, I.C.S., of Dharwar, Rao Saheb Abraham Pandither, and his accomplished daughters from Tanjore and last, but not least, Mr. Bhatkande.
I may also mention that the Durbars of Udaipur, Alwar, Jaipur, Bhavnagar, Indore, Kolhapur, Gwalior, Rampur, Hyderabad, Bikanir and Mysore have shown a profound interest and appreciation of our labour and some of them have also deputed their best artists to the Conference. With these words I request Your Highness to declare the Conference open.”
H.H.the Gaekwar in declaring the Conference open said :-
“Music like other sciences and arts exercises a potent influence on the social and intellectual development of a nation. The revival of Indian music is sure to yield good results. Music is a useful acquisition to the rich and the poor, the rulers and the ruled. I thank all those who have come here from various parts of the country and wish hearty success to the work undertaken by them.”
The Dewan, as Chairman of the Committee, proposed in suitable words that Thakur Nawab Ali Khan Akbarpur be elected President of the Conference. Mr. A.M. Masani, the Minister of Education, seconded the proposal.
The President’s Speech
Thakur Nawab Ali Khan of Akbarpur having been elected President of the Conference addressed the assembly.
After thanking the Managing Committee of the Conference for the great honour they had done by electing him President of the Conference, and referring to the enlightened liberality and profound culture of H.H. the Gaekwar, which made it possible for all votaries of the art to come together in his capital, to deliberate upon a subject which is so dear to their hearts, the President said :-
“We must look at such a Conference from the point of view of Indian unity. Men from North and South and East and West have come to compare their experiences together and to contribute materially to the success of the Conference and in the midst of Babel of languages, we can still mingle freely with the aid of the common language of music. Secondly, no one will deny that the music of the country is at present in the hands of an ignorant and illiterate class and that it is essential to rescue it from the possibility of complete destruction and place it on a scientific basis.
In the little pamphlet sent to me by your energetic Secretary Professor Joshi, I notice that he refers to music as a potent instrument in expressing the soul of nation. I shall not take up your time in dealing with the spiritual side of music nor stand long between yourself and the great experts who are here to give us the benefit of their advice. I must, however, utter a word of caution. It is of the greatest importance that the deliberations of the Conference should be conducted in a friendly spirit in order that a definite step forward may be taken and the cause of Indian music substantially advanced.
There will, doubtless, be differences of opinion even on fundamental questions connected with Indian music and there is therefore likely to result a friendly clash of arms between the advocates of different theories, but I would earnestly request the members who are about to take part in the discussions not to lose sight of the central object of our work. It is, of course, open to the members of the Conference to suggest various lines of action which seem necessary in order to give a permanent form and continuity to this important movement for the emancipation of Indian music.
The President then called upon Mr. V.N. Bhatknande to read his Paper on “A historical survey of Hindustani music, its present condition, and the means to improve it and place it on a scientific foundation, with a view to make its study as easy as possible.”
In the evening sessions of the Conference papers were read by Mr. E.Clements on “The intonation of Indian Music,” and by Rao Bahadur K.B.Deval on “The theory of Indian music as expounded by Somanatha.”
His Highness was pleased to instruct Prof. S.L.Joshi, the Secretary to invite the members of the Conference and others to the Palace Hall at 9 p.m. to attend the demonstration of Indian music by the great masters who have been specially sent to Baroda from other States for this purpose.
